sections.title: 1. Introduction

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 1, Introduction; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 1.1. Overview

summary.text: The overview motivates the specification. It says establishing the provenance of media is critical to trust, because mis-attributed and mis-contextualised content spreads quickly on social platforms and inauthentic content is rising, and because creators cannot currently attach metadata to their work in a secure, tamper-evident and standardised way across platforms. Provenance lets creators and editors disclose how an asset was created and changed; each change is added while the existing provenance is preserved. The C2PA developed the specification to enable global, opt-in adoption of digital provenance, informed by requirements from industry experts and partners including the Project Origin Alliance and the Content Authenticity Initiative, and notes that regulators could also use it to establish standards.

sections.extract: With the increasing velocity of digital content and the increasing availability of powerful creation and editing techniques, establishing the provenance of media is critical to ensure transparency, understanding, and ultimately, trust. We are witnessing extraordinary challenges to trust in media. As social platforms amplify the reach and influence of certain content via ever more complex and opaque algorithms,

sections.title: 1.2. Scope

summary.text: The scope: the specification describes the technical side of the C2PA architecture, a model for storing and accessing cryptographically verifiable information whose trustworthiness is assessed against a defined trust model, including how to create and process a C2PA Manifest and how digital signatures provide tamper-evidence and trust. It was written after the C2PA's Guiding Principles, which focus on privacy and personal control of data and on potential abuse; implementers are strongly encouraged to let creators and publishers control whether certain provenance data is included. Quoting those principles, it says C2PA specifications do not judge provenance data as good or bad, only whether its assertions validate as bound to the asset, well-formed and untampered. The specification should not harm content accessibility, and other C2PA documents cover user experience and threat and harms modelling.

sections.extract: This specification describes the technical aspects of the C2PA architecture; a model for storing and accessing cryptographically verifiable information whose trustworthiness can be assessed based on a defined trust model. Included in this document is information about how to create and process a C2PA Manifest and its components, including the use of digital signature technology for enabling tamper-evidence as well

sections.title: 1.3. Technical Overview

summary.text: The technical overview: C2PA information is a series of statements, called assertions, about matters such as asset creation, edit actions, capture device details and bindings to content; together they make up an asset's provenance and act as trust signals for a human. Assertions are wrapped with further information into a claim, which the claim generator signs on behalf of the signer with the signer's credential, producing the claim signature. A claim generator (hardware or software) binds the assertions, claim and claim signature into a verifiable unit, the C2PA Manifest (Figure 1), and the set of C2PA Manifests stored in the asset's Content Credential is its provenance data.

sections.extract: The C2PA information comprises a series of statements that cover areas such as asset creation, edit actions, capture device details, bindings to content and many other subjects. These statements, called assertions, make up the provenance of a given asset and represent a series of trust signals that can be used by a human to improve their view of trustworthiness concerning the asset. sections.title: 1.3.1. Establishing Trust

summary.text: Trust in C2PA rests on the identity of the signer associated with the key used to sign a claim, per the specification's trust model. Combined with trusted time stamps, claim signatures can be validated indefinitely to determine whether a claim was signed while the signing credentials were valid and not revoked.

sections.extract: The basis of making trust decisions in C2PA, our trust model, is the identity of the signer associated with the cryptographic signing key used to sign a claim in a C2PA Manifest. The claim signatures of C2PA Manifests, when combined with trusted time stamps, can undergo the validation process indefinitely to determine if claims were signed while the signing credentials were valid and not revoked. <a

sections.title: 1.3.2. An Example

summary.text: A worked example: a C2PA-enabled camera or phone takes a photograph and creates a manifest whose assertions include details about the camera, a thumbnail and cryptographic hashes binding the photograph to the manifest. The assertions are listed in a claim, which is digitally signed, and the whole C2PA Manifest (Figure 2) is embedded in the output JPEG, where it remains valid indefinitely. A manifest consumer such as a validator then validates the signature and its credential, checks each assertion, and presents the information and signature so the user can make an informed decision about the content's trustworthiness.

sections.extract: A very common scenario will be a user taking a photograph with their C2PA-enabled camera (or phone). In that instance, the camera would create a manifest containing some assertions including information about the camera itself, a thumbnail of the image and some cryptographic hashes that bind the photograph to the manifest. sections.title: 1.3.3. Design Goals

summary.text: The design goals, listed in Table 1 so the technology works across hardware and software worldwide and is accessible to all: privacy (users control their information), responsibility (consumers can determine provenance), scalability (web-scale creation and validation), extensibility (others can add metadata and credentials without C2PA approval), interoperability, whole-workflow applicability (provenance kept from creation through publication), technology minimalism (rely on well-established techniques), security (trustworthy integrity and source, with expert review), content ubiquity (all common media types, including documents), flexible locality (online and offline), global universality, accessibility (e.g. WCAG), harms and misuse (avert harms, including to human rights and vulnerable groups), and evolving (continual review against these goals).

sections.extract: In the creation of the C2PA architecture, it was important to establish some clear goals for the work to ensure that the technology was usable across a wide spectrum of hardware and software implementations worldwide and accessible to all. sections.title: 1.4. How to Read This Specification

summary.text: Reading guidance: the specification is easier to read in the parts relevant to one's role, in a useful order, than from start to finish. It lists three roles, each with its own section: claim generators (1.5), validators (1.6) and security reviewers (1.7).

sections.extract: Before reading this specification, it’s helpful to determine which parts of the specification apply to your role. It’s easier to read the spec in relevant parts and in a useful order rather than as a whole from start to finish. Below are common roles and the sections most relevant to them, listed in the order it’s most helpful to read them. Section 1.5, “Claim Generators” Section 1.6, “Validators” Section 1.7,

sections.title: 1.5. Claim Generators

summary.text: A reading path for claim generators, whose core flow is to create assertions, reference them from a claim, include relevant ingredients, bind the claim to the asset, sign it, and package everything as a valid C2PA Manifest; examples are cameras, recorders, AI asset creators, editing software and transcoders. Required reading, each with its reason: the Technical Overview; selected Glossary terms; Assertions; Unique Identifiers (C2PA URNs); Binding to Content (hard bindings, and soft bindings such as watermarks for recovering a stripped manifest); Claims; URI References; Manifests; Embedding C2PA Manifests (only the supported formats); the standard assertions the generator emits; Cryptography; and parts of the Trust Model. Live Media is required only for live content, and Validation only for generators that support ingredients, since ingredients must be validated on ingestion — though any generator can use it as a QA checklist.

sections.extract: The core implementation flow for Claim Generators is to create assertions, reference them from a claim, include relevant ingredients, bind the claim to the asset, sign the claim, and package everything into a valid C2PA Manifest. Examples of Claim Generators in the C2PA ecosystem include cameras, recorders, AI asset creators, asset editing software, and transcoders. Must Read to Implement a Claim Generator Technical

sections.title: 1.6. Validators

summary.text: A reading path for validators, whose core flow is to locate the C2PA Manifest Store, identify the active manifest, validate the claim and signature, check signer trust and credential status, validate assertions, ingredients and the content binding, and return or display the results; examples are photo galleries, social media platforms, news publishers and verification tools. Required reading: the Technical Overview; selected Glossary terms; parts of Manifests; hard and soft bindings; hashing and signatures in Cryptography; parts of the Trust Model (validation states, trust lists, X.509 certificates); all of Validation, the core validator section; and the standard assertions the product handles. User Experience is needed only when results are shown to users, so as not to mislead them, and Live Media only for live content. Embedding, Assertions, Claims and URI References are listed as helpful context on the data structures.

sections.extract: The core implementation flow for validators is to locate the C2PA Manifest Store, identify the active manifest, validate the claim and signature, check signer trust and credential status, validate assertions and ingredients, validate the asset’s content binding, and return or display validation results. Examples of validators in the C2PA ecosystem include photo gallery applications, social media platforms, news

sections.title: 1.7. Security Reviewers

summary.text: A reading path for security reviewers, who check whether the trust model, cryptographic algorithms, validation process and security guidance meet current best practice. Required reading: the Design Goals (including what the specification is and is not meant to prove), the Technical Overview, Information Security Considerations (the core section, on threats, harms, misuse and abuse), the Trust Model, Cryptography and Validation. Helpful context: Assertions, Binding to Content (including the risks when assets are modified, stripped or matched by soft binding), Claims, Manifests (integrity, ambiguity, stripping and substitution risks), the relevant embedding formats, and the standard assertions relevant to the reviewer's threat model. User Experience is needed when reviewing user-facing trust signals, since misleading presentation can undermine security claims, and Live Media when reviewing live workflows.

sections.extract: Security reviewers inspect the various specifications and guidance documents from the C2PA to determine whether the trust model, cryptographic algorithms, validation process, and security guidance meet current best practices. sections.title: 2. Glossary

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 2, Glossary; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 2.1. Introductory terms

summary.text: Heading for Section 2.1, Introductory terms; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 2.1.1. Actor

summary.text: Defines an actor as a human or non-human (hardware or software) participant in the C2PA ecosystem, such as a camera, image editing software, a cloud service or the person using them. A note adds that an organisation or group of actors may also count as an actor.

sections.extract: A human or non-human (hardware or software) that is participating in the C2PA ecosystem. For example: a camera (capture device), image editing software, cloud service or the person using such tools. NOTE: An organization or group of actors may also be considered an actor in the C2PA ecosystem.

sections.title: 2.1.2. Claim generator

summary.text: Defines the claim generator as the non-human (hardware or software) actor that generates the claim about an asset and the claim signature, leading to the asset's C2PA Manifest. A note says it is a component of a larger system, such as a library, SDK or shared service that a signer relies on, and is not the signer, so it does not take responsibility for the content of the claim or its assertions.

sections.extract: The non-human (hardware or software) actor that generates the claim about an asset as well as the claim signature, thus leading to the asset's associated C2PA Manifest. NOTE: The claim generator is a component of a larger system, such as a library, software development kit (SDK), or shared service that a signer relies on to generate and embed claims in assets, but is not the Signer itself and thus does not assume

sections.title: 2.1.3. Signer

summary.text: Defines the signer as the holder of the credential whose private key is used to sign the claim; the signer is identified by the subject of that credential.

sections.extract: The credential holder of a private key that is used to sign the claim. The signer is identified by the subject of the credential.

sections.title: 2.1.4. Manifest consumer

summary.text: Defines a manifest consumer as an actor that consumes an asset with an associated C2PA Manifest in order to obtain the provenance data from that manifest.

sections.extract: An actor who consumes an asset with an associated C2PA Manifest for the purpose of obtaining the provenance data from the C2PA Manifest.

sections.title: 2.1.5. Validator

summary.text: Defines a validator as a manifest consumer whose role is to perform the actions described in the specification's validation section.

sections.extract: A Manifest Consumer whose role is to perform the actions described in validation.

sections.title: 2.1.6. Action

summary.text: Defines an action as an operation performed by an actor on an asset, with examples "create", "embed" and "apply filter".

sections.extract: An operation performed by an actor on an asset. For example, "create", "embed", or "apply filter".

sections.title: 2.2. Assets and Content

summary.text: Heading for Section 2.2, Assets and Content; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 2.2.1. Digital content

summary.text: Defines digital content as the part of an asset that is the actual content, such as an image's pixels, together with any technical metadata needed to understand it, such as a colour profile or encoding parameters.

sections.extract: The portion of an asset that represents the actual content, such as the pixels of an image, along with any additional technical metadata required to understand the content (e.g., a colour profile or encoding parameters).

sections.title: 2.2.2. Asset metadata

summary.text: Defines asset metadata as non-technical information about an asset and its digital content.

sections.extract: Non-technical information about the asset and its digital content.

sections.title: 2.2.3. Asset

summary.text: Defines an asset as a file or stream of data containing digital content, asset metadata and, optionally, a C2PA Manifest. A note extends "file" here to include cloud-native and dynamically generated data.

sections.extract: A file or stream of data containing digital content, asset metadata and optionally, a C2PA Manifest. NOTE: For the purposes of this definition, we will extend the typical definition of "file" to include cloud-native and dynamically generated data.

sections.title: 2.2.4. Derived asset

summary.text: Defines a derived asset as one created from an existing asset by performing actions that modify its digital content, for example a shortened audio stream or a document with added pages.

sections.extract: A derived asset is an asset that is created by starting from an existing asset and performing actions to it that modify its digital content. EXAMPLE: An audio stream that has been shortened or a document where pages have been added.

sections.title: 2.2.5. Asset rendition

summary.text: Defines an asset rendition as a representation of an asset, either part of it or a wholly new asset, whose digital content has undergone a non-editorial transformation such as re-encoding or scaling; the example is a video re-encoded for a lower screen resolution or bandwidth.

sections.extract: A representation of an asset (either as a part of an asset or a completely new asset) where the digital content has had a 'non-editorial transformation' action (e.g., re-encoding or scaling) applied. EXAMPLE: A video file that is re-encoded for reduced screen resolution or network bandwidth.

sections.title: 2.2.6. Composed asset

summary.text: Defines a composed asset as one built from a collection of parts or fragments of digital content, called ingredients, taken from one or more other assets. When it starts from an existing asset it is a special case of a derived asset, but it can also start from a blank slate. Examples are a video assembled from imported clips and audio segments, and an image with another image superimposed on it.

sections.extract: A composed asset is an asset that is created by building up a collection of multiple parts or fragments of digital content (referred to as ingredients) from one or more other assets. When starting from an existing asset, it is a special case of a derived asset - however a composed asset can also be one that starts from a "blank slate". EXAMPLES: A video created by importing existing video clips and audio segments

sections.title: 2.2.7. Editorial transformation

summary.text: Defines an editorial transformation as one that alters the intent or the meaning (or both) of the digital content. A note says every editorial transformation is perceptible, but not every perceptible transformation is editorial.

sections.extract: A type of transformation that alters either the intent or meaning or both of the digital content. NOTE: Every editorial transformation is a perceptible transformation, but not every perceptible transformation is editorial

sections.title: 2.2.8. Perceptible transformation

summary.text: Defines a perceptible transformation as one that alters how humans perceive the digital content under normal conditions.

sections.extract: A type of transformation that alters how the digital content is perceived by humans under normal conditions.

sections.title: 2.3. Core Aspects of C2PA

summary.text: Heading for Section 2.3, Core Aspects of C2PA; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 2.3.1. Assertion

summary.text: Defines an assertion as a data structure representing a statement about the asset, either made by the signer or simply gathered when the claim is generated; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.

sections.extract: A data structure which represents a statement either made (or "created") by the signer or simply gathered at claim generation-time, concerning the asset. This data is a part of the C2PA Manifest.

sections.title: 2.3.2. Assertion store

summary.text: Defines the assertion store as the logical collection of assertions that a claim references within a C2PA Manifest, stored together as one construct, and points to the Assertion Store section for its full structure.

sections.extract: The logical collection of assertions referenced by a claim within a C2PA Manifest, stored together as a single construct. For the full structural description, see Assertion Store.

sections.title: 2.3.3. Claim

summary.text: Defines a claim as a digitally signed, tamper-evident data structure that references a set of assertions about an asset and the information needed to represent the content binding, and that declares any redacted assertions; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.

sections.extract: A digitally signed and tamper-evident data structure that references a set of assertions, concerning an asset, and the information necessary to represent the content binding. If any assertions were redacted, then a declaration to that effect is included. This data is a part of the C2PA Manifest.

sections.title: 2.3.4. Claim signature

summary.text: Defines the claim signature as the digital signature on the claim, made with the private key owned by a signer; it is part of the C2PA Manifest.

sections.extract: The digital signature on the claim created using the private key owned by a signer. The claim signature is a part of the C2PA Manifest.

sections.title: 2.3.5. C2PA Manifest

summary.text: Defines a C2PA Manifest as the set of provenance information about an asset formed by one or more assertions (including content bindings), a single claim and a claim signature; it is part of a C2PA Manifest Store. A note says a manifest can reference other manifests.

sections.extract: The set of information about the provenance of an asset based on the combination of one or more assertions (including content bindings), a single claim, and a claim signature. A C2PA Manifest is part of a C2PA Manifest Store. NOTE: A C2PA Manifest can reference other C2PA Manifests.

sections.title: 2.3.6. C2PA Manifest Store

summary.text: Defines a C2PA Manifest Store as a collection of C2PA Manifests that can be embedded in an asset or kept external to it.

sections.extract: A collection of C2PA Manifests that can either be embedded into an asset or be external to its asset.

sections.title: 2.3.7. Content Credential

summary.text: Defines Content Credential as the preferred non-technical term for a C2PA Manifest, so an asset's manifest store represents its Content Credentials. The term also names the C2PA technology as a whole and is treated as a plural noun: one manifest is a Content Credential, while several manifests or the broader concept are Content Credentials.

sections.extract: This is the preferred non-technical term for a C2PA Manifest. The C2PA Manifest Store therefore represents the Content Credentials of an asset. Content Credentials also refers to the overall C2PA technology, and is therefore essentially treated as a plural noun. If a C2PA Manifest is a Content Credential, then multiple C2PA Manifest or the broader, universal concept is Content Credentials. <a

sections.title: 2.3.8. Active Manifest

summary.text: Defines the active manifest as the last manifest in a C2PA Manifest Store's list, the one whose content bindings can be validated, and points to the Manifest Store section for its full structure.

sections.extract: The last manifest in the list of C2PA Manifests inside of a C2PA Manifest Store which is the one with the set of content bindings that are able to be validated. For the full structural description, see Manifest Store.

sections.title: 2.3.9. Provenance

summary.text: Defines provenance as the logical concept of understanding an asset's history and its interactions with actors and other assets, as represented by the provenance data.

sections.extract: The logical concept of understanding the history of an asset and its interaction with actors and other assets, as represented by the provenance data.

sections.title: 2.3.10. Provenance data

summary.text: Defines provenance data as the set of C2PA Manifests for an asset and, for a composed asset, for its ingredients, and points to the Manifests section for its full structure. A note says a manifest can reference other manifests.

sections.extract: The set of C2PA Manifests for an asset and, in the case of a composed asset, its ingredients. For the full structural description, see Manifests. NOTE: A C2PA Manifest can reference other C2PA Manifests.

sections.title: 2.3.11. Authenticity

summary.text: Defines authenticity as a property of digital content comprising a set of facts, such as the provenance data and hard bindings, that can be cryptographically verified as not having been tampered with.

sections.extract: A property of digital content comprising a set of facts (such as the provenance data and hard bindings) that can be cryptographically verified as not having been tampered with.

sections.title: 2.3.12. Content binding

summary.text: Defines content binding as information that associates digital content to a specific C2PA Manifest associated with a specific asset, either as a hard binding or a soft binding; the full structural description is in the Binding to Content section.

sections.extract: Information that associates digital content to a specific C2PA Manifest associated with a specific asset, either as a hard binding or a soft binding. For the full structural description, see Binding to Content.

sections.title: 2.3.13. Hard binding

summary.text: Defines a hard binding as one or more cryptographic hashes that uniquely identify either the entire asset or a portion of it.

sections.extract: One or more cryptographic hashes that uniquely identifies either the entire asset or a portion thereof.

sections.title: 2.3.14. Soft binding

summary.text: Defines a soft binding as a content identifier that is either not statistically unique, such as a fingerprint, or embedded as an invisible watermark in the identified digital content.

sections.extract: A content identifier that is either (a) not statistically unique, such as a fingerprint, or (b) embedded as an invisible watermark in the identified digital content.

sections.title: 2.3.15. Trust signals

summary.text: Defines trust signals as the collection of information that can inform a Manifest Consumer's judgment of the trustworthiness of an asset, in addition to the signer on which the fundamental trust model relies.

sections.extract: The collection of information that can inform a Manifest Consumer’s judgment of the trustworthiness of an asset. These are in addition to the signer upon which the fundamental trust model relies.

sections.title: 2.3.16. C2PA Trust List

summary.text: Defines the C2PA Trust List as a C2PA-managed list of X.509 certificate trust anchors that issue certificates to hardware and software signers, who use them to sign claims.

sections.extract: A C2PA-managed list of X.509 certificate trust anchors that issue certificates to hardware & software signers that use them to sign claims.

sections.title: 2.3.17. C2PA TSA Trust List

summary.text: Defines the C2PA TSA Trust List as a C2PA-managed list of X.509 certificate trust anchors that issue certificates to Time Stamping Authorities (TSAs).

sections.extract: A C2PA-managed list of X.509 certificate trust anchors that issue certificates to Time Stamping Authorities (TSAs).

sections.title: 2.4. Additional Terms

summary.text: Heading that opens section 2.4 Additional Terms; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 2.4.1. Durable Content Credential

summary.text: Defines a Durable Content Credential as a Content Credential for which one or more soft bindings exist that enable its discovery in a manifest repository.

sections.extract: A Durable Content Credential is a Content Credential for which there exists one or more soft bindings that enable its discovery in a manifest repository.

sections.title: 2.4.2. Fingerprint

summary.text: Defines a fingerprint as a set of inherent properties computable from digital content that identifies the content or near duplicates of it. An example notes that if an asset becomes separated from its C2PA Manifest through removal or corruption of its metadata, a fingerprint of its digital content could be used to search a database and recover the asset with an intact C2PA Manifest.

sections.extract: A set of inherent properties computable from digital content that identifies the content or near duplicates of it. EXAMPLE: An asset can become separated from its C2PA Manifest due to removal or corruption of asset metadata. A fingerprint of the digital content of the asset could be used to search a database to recover the asset with an intact C2PA Manifest.

sections.title: 2.4.3. Invisible Watermark

summary.text: Defines an invisible watermark as information incorporated in a substantially human-imperceptible way into the digital content of an asset, which can be used, for example, to uniquely identify the asset or to store a reference to a C2PA Manifest.

sections.extract: Information incorporated in a substantially human imperceptible way into the digital content of an asset which can be used, for example, to uniquely identify the asset or to store a reference to a C2PA Manifest.

sections.title: 2.4.4. Visible Watermark

summary.text: Defines a visible watermark as a perceptible component of the digital content carrying some human-consumable information about the provenance of the asset.

sections.extract: A perceptible component of the digital content carrying some human consumable information about the provenance of the asset.

sections.title: 2.4.5. Manifest Repository

summary.text: Defines a manifest repository as a repository into which C2PA Manifests and C2PA Manifest Stores can be placed, and which can be searched using a content binding.

sections.extract: A repository into which C2PA Manifests and C2PA Manifest Stores can be placed, and which can be searched using a content binding.

sections.title: 4. Standard Terms

summary.text: Specifies that the key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14, RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 when they appear in any casing. States that CDDL rules and type definitions in the C2PA CDDL schemas are normative while comments within them are non-normative, and that schema validation is neither necessary nor recommended. If the CDDL schema conflicts with the normative text of the specification, the normative text takes precedence.

sections.title: 5. Versioning

summary.text: Heading that opens section 5 Versioning; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 5.1. Compatibility

summary.text: Describes how constructs such as box labels, assertions, claims and time stamps have evolved, and defines a deprecated construct as one that a claim generator shall not write but that a validator should read. Recommends that a claim generator declare the specification version it used by providing a specVersion key in the claim_generator_info field, which declares that the active manifest was produced per that version and contains no constructs deprecated in it. Requires a validator to be compatible with at least one specification version and to support all non-deprecated constructs of any version it is compatible with, while allowing it to ignore constructs it does not support (deprecated or unknown) and process the rest of the C2PA Manifest. Also recommends that a claim generator performing ingredient validation add a specVersion key to the validation-results-map to declare the version used for the validation procedure.

sections.extract: As the Content Credentials specification has evolved, constructs such as box labels, assertions (and their fields), claims and time stamps have also evolved. New assertions have been added, and some existing assertions and the claim have newer versions with additional fields. In addition, some constructs have been deprecated. In this specification, when a construct is marked as deprecated, that means that a claim

sections.title: 5.2. Forward Compatibility

summary.text: Describes the C2PA aim that Content Credentials created under newer specification versions remain parseable and validatable by implementations of earlier versions wherever practical. Recommends that implementations gracefully handle unknown or unrecognized data without fatal errors, preserve the integrity of a C2PA Manifest even when parts of it cannot be fully interpreted, and indicate partial interpretation to users or downstream systems rather than rejecting the manifest outright. Notes that breaking changes may occasionally be necessary for significant advances or fundamental security, trust or interoperability concerns, in which case versioning guidance and migration considerations will be explicitly documented.

sections.extract: C2PA aims to ensure that Content Credentials created under newer versions of the specification remains parseable and validatable when processed by implementations conforming to earlier versions, wherever practical. Implementations of the C2PA specification should therefore be designed to: Gracefully handle unknown or unrecognized data (e.g., new fields, structures, or claim types) without causing fatal errors.

sections.title: 5.3. Version History

summary.text: Points to the Version History appendix for a detailed version history of the specification.

sections.extract: A detailed version history of this specification can be found in the Version History appendix of this document.

sections.title: 7. Entity Diagram

summary.text: Presents Figure 4, the C2PA Entity Diagram, showing how the parts of the C2PA system integrate and relate to each other. It explains that an asset embeds a C2PA Manifest Store holding one or more C2PA Manifests, the last of which is the active manifest whose content bindings are validated against the asset's digital content. Within each manifest, the assertion store collects the assertions (including any ingredient assertions and the content binding), and the claim references them by URI and is cryptographically signed by the claim signature. Green lines in the diagram denote containment and blue lines denote logical references, and the Manifests, Assertions, Claims and Binding to Content sections give the full structural descriptions.

sections.title: 8. Assertions

summary.text: Heading that opens section 8 Assertions; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 8.1. General

summary.text: Describes the expectation that each claim generator creates or assembles one or more assertions about when, where and how an asset was originated or transformed, and defines an assertion as labelled data, typically but not necessarily in a CBOR-based structure, representing a declaration about an asset. Notes that some assertions contain human-generated information and others machine-generated information, with examples including metadata, actions performed on the asset, thumbnails of the asset or its ingredients, and content bindings. States that assertions may be redacted by subsequent claims (Section 8.8 Redaction of Assertions) but cannot be modified once made as part of a claim.

sections.extract: It is expected that each claim generator, used by actors in the system that creates or processes an asset, will create or assemble one or more assertions about when, where, and how the asset was originated or transformed. An assertion is labelled data, typically (though not required to be) in a CBOR-based structure which represents a declaration about an asset. Some of these assertions will contain human-generated

sections.title: 8.2. Labels

summary.text: Heading that opens section 8.2 Labels; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 8.2.1. Namespacing

summary.text: Specifies that string values in C2PA data structures may be organized into namespaces using a period as a separator, that any string value defined in the specification shall begin with the c2pa namespace, and that the C2PA namespace registry lists other top-level namespaces. Requires entity-specific namespaces (any other than c2pa or registered ones) to begin with the entity's Internet domain name starting with a valid IANA top-level domain, similar to Java packages (e.g. com.litware), so that labels defined by different entities do not collide. Requires the period-separated components of an entity-specific namespace to follow the POSIX or C locale variable naming convention [a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*, and gives an ABNF for namespaces.

sections.extract: String values in C2PA data structures may be organized into namespaces using a period (.) as a separator. The C2PA namespace, c2pa, shall be the beginning of any string value defined in this specification. In addition to the c2pa namespace, the C2PA namespace registry lists other top-level namespaces. Entity-specific namespaces, meaning any namespace other than c2pa or those on the registry, shall begin with the

sections.title: 8.2.2. Label Naming

summary.text: Describes assertion labels as namespaced strings defined by the C2PA specifications or an external entity, most commonly in the c2pa namespace, and versioned with a simple incrementing integer such as c2pa.actions.v2, where a missing version is considered v1. Points to Chapter 16 C2PA Standard Assertions for publicly known labels, and notes that namespacing for well-established standards is now done through entity-specific namespaces such as org.iso and org.w3. Gives an ABNF for assertion labels and states that label components follow the POSIX or C locale variable naming convention [a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*, with a repeated underscore (__) reserved for labelling multiple assertions of the same type.

sections.extract: Each assertion has a label defined either by the C2PA specifications or an external entity. These labels are strings which are namespaced, as described in the preceding clause or by an entity. The most common labels will be defined in the c2pa namespace, but labels may use any namespace that follows the conventions. Labels are also versioned with a simple incrementing integer scheme (e.g., c2pa.actions.v2). If no

sections.title: 8.3. Versioning

summary.text: Recommends that changes to an assertion's schema be backwards compatible, so new fields may be added and existing ones marked deprecated (read but never written), while existing fields shall not be removed and the label takes an incremented version number, e.g. moving from c2pa.actions to c2pa.actions.v2. Optional fields may be added without changing the version number. Requires deprecated fields of C2PA standard assertions to be indicated in Chapter 16 C2PA Standard Assertions and forbids claim generators from inserting data into deprecated fields. Requires a non-backwards-compatible change to give the assertion a new label rather than a higher version number, such as the fictional c2pa.component replacing c2pa.ingredient.

sections.extract: When an assertion’s schema is changed, it should be done in a backwards-compatible manner. This means that new fields may be added and existing ones may be marked as deprecated (i.e., can be read, but never written). Existing fields shall not be removed. The label would then consist of an incremented version number, for example moving from c2pa.actions (deprecated) to c2pa.actions.v2. Since the addition of optional

sections.title: 8.4. Multiple Instances

summary.text: Specifies that multiple assertions of the same type in one manifest are given unique labels by appending a double underscore and a monotonically increasing index, e.g. c2pa.metadata, c2pa.metadata__1 and c2pa.metadata__2. When a label includes a version number, the instance number follows the versioned label, e.g. c2pa.ingredient.v2__2.

sections.extract: Multiple assertions of the same type can occur in the same manifest, but since assertions are referenced by claims via their label, the assertion labels are required to be unique. This is accomplished by adding a double-underscore and a monotonically increasing index to the label. For example, if a manifest contains a single assertion of type c2pa.metadata, then the assertion label will be c2pa.metadata. If a

sections.title: 8.5. Schema Validation

summary.text: Recommends that claim generators use the schemas in the document and the machine-readable ones from the C2PA website to ensure their assertions are consistent with the expected structures, noting that the schemas also aid understanding of the syntax. States that validators should not validate inputs against these schemas.

sections.extract: The schemas provided in this document, as well as the machine readable ones that can be downloaded from the C2PA website, should be used by claim generators to ensure that the assertions they create are consistent with the expected structures. These schemas can also be used as aids in understanding the syntax to be read or written. Validators should not validate inputs against these schemas. <a

sections.title: 8.6. Assertion Store

summary.text: Defines the assertion store as the logical collection of assertions referenced by a claim in a manifest, which shall be stored as described in Section 11.5 Serialization. Requires each assertion referenced in a claim's created_assertions or gathered_assertions (but not redacted_assertions) to be present in the assertion store of the same C2PA Manifest as the claim. Notes that each manifest has a single assertion store but an asset may have several, and recommends that each assertion include a randomly-generated salt in the private c2sh box within its JUMBF Description Box (Section 9.4.2.3 Hashing JUMBF Boxes) so subsequent generators can redact assertions securely.

sections.extract: The set of assertions referenced by a claim in a manifest are collected together into a logical construct that is referred to as the assertion store. The assertions and assertion store shall be stored as described in Section 11.5, “Serialization”; in particular, each assertion referenced in a claim’s created_assertions or gathered_assertions (but not redacted_assertions) shall be present in the assertion store

sections.title: 8.7. Embedded vs Externally-Stored Data

summary.text: Describes how assertion data that is large or infrequently needed may be hosted externally and referenced by URI instead of being embedded in the assertion store, using either a cloud data assertion for remotely stored C2PA assertions (JUMBF) or an external reference assertion for remotely stored assertion or non-assertion data. In both cases the externally hosted data is not retrieved or validated as part of manifest validation, and is only retrieved and validated when an application specifically needs it, under the rules in Section 14.10 Validate the Assertions.

sections.extract: Some assertion data, due to its size or an infrequent need for it, may be externally hosted. Such data are not embedded in the assertion store, but instead are referenced by URI. This is accomplished through either a cloud data assertion for remotely-stored C2PA assertions (JUMBF) or an external reference assertion for either remotely stored assertion or non-assertion data. In both cases, the externally hosted data

sections.title: 8.8. Redaction of Assertions

summary.text: Defines redaction as removing assertions from an asset-embedded manifest when the asset is used as an ingredient, and requires it to be done either by removing the entire assertion from the assertion store or by replacing its content per Section 14.10.3 Redacted Assertion Representation. Requires a URI reference to the redacted assertion in the claim's redacted_assertions field, strongly recommends a c2pa.redacted action with a redacted field, and requires an ingredient manifest to be removed from the C2PA Manifest Store when redacting its ingredient assertion leaves no other references to it; because the URI includes the assertion label, the type of removed information remains known. Recommends documenting a redaction with an update manifest unless it accompanies changes to data covered by content bindings. Forbids claim generators from redacting c2pa.actions or c2pa.actions.v2 assertions, and from redacting the hard binding assertion for the current asset when creating an update manifest; validator handling is described in Section 14.10 Validate the Assertions.

sections.extract: Assertions that are present in an asset-embedded manifest may be removed from that asset’s manifest when the asset is used as an ingredient. This process is called redaction. Redaction shall be performed either by removing the entire assertion from the manifest’s assertion store or by replacing its content, as described in Section 14.10.3, “Redacted Assertion Representation”. In addition, a record that something was

sections.title: 8.9. Specifications of time in assertions

summary.text: Specifies that the default date/time value in an assertion is serialized as CBOR tag 0 and represented in CDDL as tdate, which requires an explicit timezone or Z. Distinguishes the evidentiary meanings of standard time values (the signer's claim of the time), a claimed time of signing (signer-claimed and not independently authoritative), and a trusted time stamp (TSA evidence about the data submitted to it). Specifies that claim generator timestamp fields use generator-lower-bound-time-type or generator-upper-bound-time-type, taking a direct tdate or a map with a tdate in value and an optional timeStampType, and that a value without timeStampType shall be interpreted as absolute; lowerBound and upperBound give bounds without guaranteeing the actual time and, on start and end fields, bracket when the process or action occurred. Notes that the claimed time of signing uses CBOR tag 1 (seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00Z), that the time stamp assertion uses standard time-stamping formats, and that the different representations allow the most appropriate standards-based form for each use case.

sections.extract: The default specification for a date/time value in an assertion is the date/time format which is serialized in CBOR as tag number 0 (RFC 8949, 3.4.1) and represented in CDDL as type tdate. NOTE: CBOR Tag 0 is described in RFC 8949 as "the date-time production in RFC 3339, as refined by Section 3.3 of RFC 4287, representing the point in time described there". sections.title: 9. Unique Identifiers

summary.text: Heading that opens section 9 Unique Identifiers; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 9.1. Uniquely Identifying C2PA Manifests and Assets

summary.text: Specifies that every C2PA Manifest is uniquely identified by a URN from the c2pa URN namespace and that a C2PA asset is identified by the c2pa URN of its active manifest. The URN consists of the required urn:c2pa identifier and UUID v4 string, optionally followed by a Claim Generator identifier (no more than 32 ASCII characters that are not control or graphic characters) and a Version and Reason string (a positive integer, an underscore and another positive integer), separated by colons. When a Version and Reason string is present, a Claim Generator identifier shall also be present but may be empty; an ABNF and examples are given. Notes that earlier versions used a UUID URN with the claim generator identifier first, which did not comply with RFC 9562 or RFC 8141, and that the c2pa URN is used, for example, to identify an asset as an ingredient.

sections.extract: Every C2PA Manifest is uniquely identified and referenced by a Uniform Resource Name RFC 8141, URNs from the c2pa URN namespace, and a C2PA asset is uniquely identified by the c2pa URN value of its active manifest. The ABNF for the C2PA URN is described by ABNF for C2PA URN. A c2pa URN shall consist of two mandatory and two optional components, in the following order, with colons (:) between each section. URN

sections.title: 9.2. Versioning Manifests Due to Conflicts

summary.text: Describes situations where a C2PA Manifest must be re-labelled due to an identifier conflict, such as an ingredient manifest with the same label but different content being added to an asset's C2PA Manifest Store, and requires the modified copy to be re-labelled. To re-label, the claim generator shall append a colon if the URN has no Claim Generator identifier string and then, in all cases, append a colon followed by a monotonically increasing integer starting at 1, an underscore, and a reason code, where 1 means conflict with another C2PA Manifest. For example, a second re-labelling due to conflict appends :2_1.

sections.extract: Situations may arise where it is necessary to re-label a C2PA Manifest due to a conflict of identifiers. For example, if a claim generator had already added an ingredient manifest into the asset’s C2PA Manifest Store, then later added another ingredient which had a manifest with the same label in its manifest store, but this latter version of the manifest was different due, for example, to a manipulation of one of

sections.title: 9.3. Identifying Non-C2PA Assets

summary.text: Requires that, for assets without a C2PA Manifest but with embedded XMP containing xmpMM:DocumentID and/or xmpMM:InstanceID, those values be used as the asset's identifiers. For assets with neither a C2PA Manifest nor embedded XMP, the claim generator may use any method of its choosing to obtain a unique identifier.

sections.extract: When working with assets that do not contain a C2PA Manifest, but the asset contains embedded XMP which include values for xmpMM:DocumentID and/or xmpMM:InstanceID as defined in XMP Specification Part 2, 2.2, those values shall be used as identifiers for the asset. sections.title: 9.4. URI References

summary.text: Heading that opens section 9.4 URI References; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 9.4.1. Standard URIs

summary.text: Requires all references to information in the manifest, whether embedded or stored externally, to use JUMBF URI references as defined in ISO 19566-5:2023, C.2, normally within a hashed_uri or hashed_ext_uri structure, and notes that the field-referencing extension in Section 16.4.1.4.6 Unique Identifiers for Actions applies only in that context. For a compressed manifest, the URI shall be formed as if the manifest were not compressed, including the label of the c2ma or c2um box but not the c2cm box, and shall not include the label of the brob box. A validator shall treat an internal JUMBF URI reference as unresolved if any label in its path is ambiguous because multiple child boxes share that label.

sections.extract: All references to information in the manifest, whether stored internally to the asset (i.e., embedded) or stored externally to the asset (e.g., in the cloud), shall be referenced via JUMBF URI references as defined in ISO 19566-5:2023, C.2. These URIs are normally used either as part of a hashed_uri or hashed_ext_uri data structure. NOTE: Section 16.4.1.4.6, “Unique Identifiers for Actions” describes an extension to

sections.title: 9.4.2. Hashed URIs

summary.text: Heading that opens section 9.4.2 Hashed URIs; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 9.4.2.1. Embedded

summary.text: Specifies that a hashed_uri is used when the URI refers to something embedded in the same C2PA Manifest Store, and gives the CDDL hashed-uri-map with a url (JUMBF URI), an optional alg, and a hash byte string. If alg is absent the algorithm is taken from an enclosing structure, the field in this structure is used if both are present, and the structure is invalid if neither supplies one. Because assertion stores shall be in the same C2PA Manifest box as the claim, only self#jumbf URIs are permitted; these may be relative to the entire C2PA Manifest Store (starting with a slash) or to the current manifest, and shall not contain the two-period sequence (..). Examples of both URI forms are given.

sections.extract: A hashed_uri is used when the URI is for something embedded in the same C2PA Manifest Store. This specification provides an equivalent hashed-uri-map data structure for schemas using a CDDL Definition (see Section G.3.1, “Hashed URI” for the complete normative schema): CDDL for hashed URI ; The data structure used to store a reference to a URL within the same JUMBF ; and its hash. We use a socket/plug here to allow

sections.title: 9.4.2.2. External

summary.text: Specifies the hashed-ext-uri-map structure for referencing resources external to the C2PA Manifest Store, a variation of hashed-uri with an http/https url, a mandatory alg, a hash, and optional dc:format, size and data_types fields. Recommends the https scheme to protect privacy in transit but also permits http because data integrity is protected by the hash field, leaving manifest authors to choose. When present, dc:format provides an alternative to the Content-Type header and shall be used as the required format during content negotiation, and data_types may give one or more asset types for more clarity. The optional size field gives the size of the data to be retrieved and may serve validators as a hint alongside the hash, for example about whether to download, validate or both.

sections.extract: When referring to a resource that exists externally to the C2PA Manifest Store, a hashed-ext-uri-map data structure is used. It is a variation on the hashed-uri, in that it references an external URI instead of a self#jumbf. The hashed-ext-uri data structure is defined by the hashed-ext-uri-map rule in the following CDDL Definition (see Section G.3.2, “Hashed External URI” for the complete normative schema): CDDL

sections.title: 9.4.2.3. Hashing JUMBF Boxes

summary.text: Requires the hash for a URI reference to any JUMBF box, such as assertions and data boxes, to be computed over the contents of the structure's JUMBF superbox, including the JUMBF Description Box and all content boxes but not the superbox header (with more detail in Section 12.1 Hashing). Defines the C2PA salt as a Private field of a JUMBF Description box whose value is a standard box with a 4-byte big-endian length, a box type of c2sh, and a payload of 16 or 32 bytes of randomly generated data. Figure 5 shows an example c2pa.actions assertion.

sections.extract: When creating a URI reference to any JUMBF box (e.g., assertions and data boxes), the hash shall be performed over the contents of the structure’s JUMBF superbox, which includes both the JUMBF Description Box and all content boxes therein (but does not include the structure’s JUMBF superbox header). NOTE: More details on hashing can be found at Section 12.1, “Hashing”. As described in the latest version of JUMBF

sections.title: 10. Claims

summary.text: Heading that opens section 10 Claims; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 10.1. Overview

summary.text: Defines a claim as gathering all the assertions about an asset at a given time, including those for binding to content, which is then cryptographically hashed and signed as described in Section 10.3.2.4 Signing a Claim. Specifies that a claim is encoded as a JUMBF superbox labelled c2pa.claim.v2 with a CBOR payload that shall comply with the CBOR Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements. Notes that assertion metadata on claims is deprecated, and that the earlier c2pa.claim label and claim-map are deprecated: validators should still accept them, but claim generators shall not produce them.

sections.extract: A claim gathers together all the assertions about an asset at a given time including the set of assertions for binding to the content. The claim is then cryptographically hashed and signed as described in Section 10.3.2.4, “Signing a Claim”. A claim is encoded as a JUMBF superbox with the label c2pa.claim.v2 and a CBOR payload, which shall comply with the Core Deterministic Encoding Requirements of CBOR (see RFC

summary.text: Heading that opens section 10.2 Syntax; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 10.2.1. Schema

summary.text: Gives the CDDL schema for claims: claim-map-v2 for the c2pa.claim.v2 label and the deprecated claim-map for c2pa.claim, with the complete normative schema in Section G.2.1 Claim. claim-map-v2 requires instanceID, claim_generator_info, signature and created_assertions, and optionally allows gathered_assertions, dc:title, redacted_assertions, alg, alg_soft, and the deprecated specVersion and metadata fields; the deprecated claim-map instead carries claim_generator, a claim_generator_info array, an assertions list and dc:format. It also defines generator-info-map with a required name and optional version, icon, operating_system, specVersion and any additional fields. An example claim-map-v2 is given in CBOR diagnostic notation.

sections.title: 10.2.2. Fields

summary.text: Specifies the claim's fields. The alg field, if present, shall be an allowed hash algorithm from Section 12.1 Hashing and applies to any hashed-uri, hard binding assertion or hash assertion that does not define its own, and if alg is absent each of those shall declare its algorithm explicitly. dc:title, if present, shall be a human-readable name for the asset, though claim generators should instead create a metadata assertion with dc:title; instanceID should be the asset's xmpMM:InstanceID when XMP is present, and otherwise some other unique identifier shall be used. The signature field shall be present with an absolute URI reference to the claim signature in the same C2PA Manifest, and created_assertions shall be present with one or more references to assertions made by the claim, attributed to the signer and including at least a hard binding assertion in a standard manifest. When present, gathered_assertions references assertions provided by other workflow components that are not attributed to the signer, and redacted_assertions references redacted assertions; the notes add that dc:format is no longer in c2pa.claim.v2, that XMP-derived field names do not require XMP, and that the claim-level specVersion is deprecated in favour of the one in claim_generator_info.

sections.extract: The alg field shall contain the hash algorithm used to compute the hash for any hashed-uri, hard binding assertion, or hash assertion that does not explicitly define it. The value of this field, if present, shall be a string that is one of the allowed hash algorithms as defined in Section 12.1, “Hashing”. sections.title: 10.2.3. Claim Generator Info

summary.text: Heading that opens section 10.2.3 Claim Generator Info; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 10.2.3.1. General

summary.text: Requires detailed information about the claim generator to be present as the value of claim_generator_info, and requires a Manifest Consumer to use that value to determine information about the claim generator for itself or for presentation in a UX. Notes that the simple-string claim_generator field of c2pa.claim is no longer present in c2pa.claim.v2.

sections.extract: Detailed information about the claim generator shall be present as the value of claim_generator_info. A Manifest Consumer shall use the value of claim_generator_info in determining information about the claim generator for itself or for presentation in a UX. NOTE: The c2pa.claim has a claim_generator field, whose value is a simple string, which is no longer present in c2pa.claim.v2.

sections.title: 10.2.3.2. Generator Info Map

summary.text: Specifies that a claim_generator_info value is a generator-info-map that shall contain a name field and may contain version, icon, or both, plus any other fields using entity-specific namespacing, and that it shall represent the non-human (hardware or software) actor that generated the claim. If present, icon shall be a hashed URI to an embedded data assertion labelled c2pa.icon that follows the multiple-instance label rules, with its hash algorithm taken from the hashed URI's alg or else the claim's alg, and Manifest Consumers should also support the data box approach of earlier versions. A specVersion field should be present and, if so, shall contain the SemVer version of the specification the claim generator used to create the manifest (e.g. 2.4.0), which validators should treat as purely informational without changing their validation logic. A JSON example is included.

sections.extract: When adding a claim_generator_info field, its value is a generator-info-map object which shall contain a name field. It may also contain either a version field or an icon field or both. In addition, any other field is permitted, using the standard entity-specific namespacing described in Section 8.2.1, “Namespacing”. summary.text: Heading that opens section 10.3 Creating a Claim; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 10.3.1. Creating Assertions

summary.text: States that before a claim can be finalized, all assertions need to be created and stored in a newly created C2PA Assertion Store. When creating a standard manifest where not all binding information is known at claim creation time, it directs use of the multiple step processing method to set up the information and fill it in later.

sections.extract: Before the claim can be finalized, all assertions need to be created and stored in a newly created C2PA Assertion Store as described later in this document. When creating a standard manifest, it may not be possible to know all of the required binding information at the time of claim creation, in which case use the multiple step processing method to setup and then later fill-in the information. <a

summary.text: Heading that opens section 10.3.2 Preparing the Claim; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 10.3.2.1. Adding Assertions and Redactions

summary.text: Requires the claim to contain a created_assertions field and allows a gathered_assertions field, whose combined values list the URI references of all assertions added to the assertion store that the claim is claiming. In a standard manifest, created_assertions shall include at least one assertion representing a hard binding. URI references to any assertions in ingredient claims that are being redacted shall be added to the redacted_assertions field.

sections.extract: The claim shall contain a created_assertions field and may contain a gathered_assertions field. The combined values from those two fields represent a list of all of the URI references for all assertions that were added to the assertion store that are being "claimed" by this claim. In a standard manifest, the created_assertions field’s value shall include at least one assertion that represents a hard binding. If any

sections.title: 10.3.2.2. Adding Ingredients

summary.text: Describes ingredients as existing assets an actor brings in to create a derived asset, composed asset or asset rendition, documented in the provenance data through ingredient assertions. Recommends inserting an ingredient's C2PA Manifests into the asset's C2PA Manifest Store, as described in Section 11.4 Ingredient Storage. If a manifest with the same unique identifier is already present, the two shall be compared: an identical new manifest shall be ignored, while a different one shall be added after its identifier is changed per Chapter 9 Unique Identifiers. If an ingredient's remote manifest cannot be retrieved, the claim generator should use the error code manifest.inaccessible.

sections.extract: In many authoring scenarios, an actor does not create an entirely new asset but instead brings in other existing assets on which to create their work - either as a derived asset, a composed asset or an asset rendition. These existing assets are called ingredients and their use is documented in the provenance data through the use of an ingredient assertion. When an ingredient contains one or more C2PA manifests,

sections.title: 10.3.2.3. Connecting the Signature

summary.text: Explains that although the signature cannot be part of the signed payload, its label is predefined, so its full URI reference is known and is set as the value of the claim's signature field. This provides the explicit binding of the claim to its signature.

sections.extract: The signature cannot be part of the signed payload, but since its label is pre-defined, then the full URI reference is also known. As such, we can include that in the claim by setting the value of the signature field of the claim to that URI reference. NOTE: This provides the explicit binding of the claim to its signature.

sections.title: 10.3.2.4. Signing a Claim

summary.text: Refers to Section 12.3 Digital Signatures for producing the signature, and requires that for both standard and update manifests the payload field of Sig_structure be the serialized CBOR of the claim document, using detached content mode. The resulting serialized COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure is written into the C2PA Claim Signature box.

sections.extract: Producing the signature is specified in Section 12.3, “Digital Signatures”. For both types of manifests, standard and update, the payload field of Sig_structure shall be the serialized CBOR of the claim document, and shall use detached content mode. The serialized COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure resulting from the digital signature procedure is written into the C2PA Claim Signature box.

sections.title: 10.3.2.5. Time Stamps

sections.title: 10.3.2.5.1. Use of RFC 3161

summary.text: Recommends that, if possible, the claim generator use an RFC 3161-compliant Time Stamping Authority to obtain a trusted time stamp proving the signature existed at a certain date and time, incorporated into the COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure as a countersignature. Encourages including time stamps because, per Chapter 14 Validation, manifests without them cease to be valid when the signing credential expires or is revoked. Requires a manifest to contain only one time stamp, noting that earlier versions allowed multiple.

sections.extract: If possible, the claim generator should use a RFC 3161-compliant Time Stamping Authority (TSA) (RFC 3161) to obtain a trusted time stamp proving that the signature itself actually existed at a certain date and time and incorporate that into the COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure as a countersignature. Claim generators are encouraged to obtain and include time stamps to ensure their manifests will remain valid. As described

sections.title: 10.3.2.5.2. Choosing the Payload

summary.text: Defines the deprecated v1 payload (in a v1 time stamp) as the same payload value used in the Sig_signature for signing the claim, which a claim generator shall not create but a validator shall process if present. Defines the v2 payload (in a v2 time stamp) as the value of the signature field of the COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure created when signing the claim, including the entire serialized bstr with its major type and length bytes, and requires claim generators to use it when time stamping.

sections.extract: A previous version of this specification used the same value for the payload field in the time stamp as was used in the Sig_signature as described in Section 10.3.2.4, “Signing a Claim”. This payload is henceforth referred to as a "v1 payload" in a "v1 time stamp" and is considered deprecated. A claim generator shall not create one, but a validator shall process one if present. sections.title: 10.3.2.5.3. Obtaining the time stamp

summary.text: Requires all time stamps to be obtained per RFC 3161 with additional requirements. The MessageImprint of the TimeStampReq shall be computed from the RFC 9052 ToBeSigned value, using a Sig_structure whose context is CounterSignature, whose payload is as described in Section 10.3.2.5.2 Choosing the Payload, and whose other elements follow Section 12.3.3 Computing the Signature. The ToBeSigned value is hashed with an algorithm from the allowed list in Section 12.1 Hashing that the TSA supports (a TSA supporting none cannot be used), preferably the same algorithm as the claim's digital signature. The certReq boolean shall be asserted so that the TSA's certificate chain is provided in the response.

The payload element shall be the value described by Section

sections.title: 10.3.2.5.4. Storing the time stamp

summary.text: Specifies that deprecated v1 time stamps are stored in a COSE unprotected header labelled sigTst whose value shall be a tstContainer, with the content of the TSA's TimeStampResp stored as the val of a tstTokens element. v2 time stamps shall be stored in a COSE unprotected header labelled sigTst2 as a tstContainer, with the timeStampToken from the TimeStampResp stored as val and formatted as a DER-encoded RFC 3161 TimeStampToken in a CBOR byte string; a note equates this to the CTT model of the IETF COSE time-stamp header draft, serving as a countersignature over the complete signature structure. If no time stamps are included, neither sigTst nor sigTst2 shall be present. The tstContainer CDDL is given and noted to be a CBOR adaptation of a subset of the JAdES schema, with val as a byte string rather than Base64.

sections.extract: v1 time stamps (deprecated) are stored in a COSE unprotected header whose label is the string sigTst. If present, the value of this header shall be a tstContainer defined by Section G.2.2, “Timestamp Container”. sections.title: 10.3.2.6. Credential Revocation Information

summary.text: Recommends that if the signer's credential supports online credential status queries and points to a service providing status information with a time stamp, the claim generator query it, capture the response, and store it as described for credentials in the Trust Model. If credential revocation information is attached this way, a trusted time stamp shall also be obtained after signing, as described in Section 10.3.2.5 Time Stamps.

sections.extract: If the signer’s credential supports querying its online credential status, and the credential contains a pointer to a service that provides credential status information with a time stamp, the claim generator should query the service, capture the response, and store it in the manner described for credentials in the Trust Model. sections.title: 11. Manifests

summary.text: Heading that opens section 11 Manifests; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 11.1. Overview

summary.text: Describes a C2PA Manifest as a container bundling an assertion store, a claim that hashes the assertions and provides information about the claim generator, and a claim signature over that claim. The manifest that describes the asset is the active manifest, and because ingredients may have their own manifests, all manifests associated with an asset are collected into a single C2PA Manifest Store. A standard C2PA Manifest includes a hard binding cryptographically associating it with the asset, so copying or linking it to a different asset is detectable and fails validation; serialization details are in Section 11.5 Serialization.

sections.extract: Within C2PA, individual statements about an asset are declared as assertions. A C2PA Manifest is a container that bundles together an assertion store holding those assertions, a claim that hashes the assertions and provides information about the claim generator, and a claim signature over that claim. The C2PA Manifest that describes the asset is called the active manifest. Because assets can be built from

sections.title: 11.2. Manifest Store

summary.text: Defines a C2PA Manifest Store as containing one or more C2PA Manifests, the last of which is the active manifest, and specifies that it is a JUMBF (ISO 19566-5:2023) superbox, with details in Section 11.5 Serialization. Figure 8 shows an example store with a single C2PA Manifest.

sections.extract: A C2PA Manifest Store contains one or more C2PA Manifests, the last of which is designated the active manifest. The C2PA Manifest Store is a JUMBF (ISO 19566-5:2023) superbox. See Section 11.5, “Serialization” for more details. Figure 8, “C2PA Manifest Store” is an example C2PA Manifest Store with a single C2PA Manifest: C2PA Manifest Store Figure 8. C2PA Manifest Store

sections.title: 11.3. Types of Manifests

summary.text: Heading that opens section 11.3 Types of Manifests; it carries no text of its own.

sections.title: 11.3.1. Common

summary.text: Requires every C2PA Manifest to contain an assertion store, a claim and a claim signature.

sections.extract: All C2PA Manifests shall contain an assertion store, a claim and a claim signature.

sections.title: 11.3.2. Standard Manifests

summary.text: Requires a standard C2PA Manifest to contain exactly one hard binding to content assertion.

sections.extract: A standard C2PA Manifest shall contain exactly one hard binding to content assertion.

sections.title: 11.3.3. Update Manifests

summary.text: Recommends an Update Manifest when assertions are added to an existing C2PA Manifest without changing the digital content or other data covered by content bindings, and forbids it from containing c2pa.hash.data, c2pa.hash.boxes, c2pa.hash.collection.data, c2pa.hash.segment, c2pa.hash.bmff.v3 or c2pa.hash.multi-asset assertions. Where the existing content binding locates the C2PA Manifest Store by file offset and length, the store shall start at the same offset after updating, though its length may change. An Update Manifest may contain c2pa.actions or c2pa.actions.v2 assertions only with the actions c2pa.edited.metadata, c2pa.opened, c2pa.published or c2pa.redacted, and shall not contain a thumbnail assertion, since other actions or a thumbnail imply changes to the digital content. It shall contain exactly one c2pa.ingredient.v3 assertion with activeManifest and claimSignature URI references to the updated asset's C2PA Manifest and Claim Signature and a relationship of parentOf, where that ingredient manifest may be a standard or update manifest.

sections.extract: In a workflow where additional assertions need to be added to an existing C2PA Manifest, but no changes are made to the digital content or other data covered by content bindings, an Update Manifest should be used. An Update Manifest shall not contain assertions of types c2pa.hash.data, c2pa.hash.boxes, c2pa.hash.collection.data, c2pa.hash.segment, c2pa.hash.bmff.v3, or c2pa.hash.multi-asset, because the content has

sections.title: 11.4. Ingredient Storage

summary.text: Describes how, when a C2PA Manifest includes ingredient assertions and an ingredient contains a C2PA Manifest Store, its C2PA Manifests are normally included in the new asset's C2PA Manifest Store to keep the provenance data intact, as described in Section 10.3.2.2 Adding Ingredients. Figure 9 shows a C2PA Manifest Store with an ingredient. Notes that the previously supported Data Box Store (c2pa.databoxes) is covered for historical reference in Section H.4 Data Box Store of Appendix H Deprecated Constructs.

sections.extract: When a C2PA Manifest includes ingredient assertions, and an ingredient contains a C2PA Manifest Store, the C2PA Manifests it contains are normally included in the C2PA Manifest Store of the new asset to ensure that the provenance data is kept intact, as described in Section 10.3.2.2, “Adding Ingredients”.
