sections.title: 16.6.8. Metadata

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.6.8, Metadata; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.6.8.1. Description

summary.text: Metadata is now represented by a category of assertions with a standardized serialization, replacing earlier per-standard assertions, so that included metadata is signed, attributable and processed consistently; these assertions may represent existing standards or private specifications.

sections.extract: In earlier versions of this specification, there were individual assertions for each metadata standard (e.g., IPTC, EXIF). In this version, there now exists a category of assertions that shall be used to represent metadata, in a standardized serialization. Having the metadata in an assertion establishes that the metadata in that assertion is significant, because it has been explicitly included in the C2PA Manifest,

sections.title: 16.6.8.2. Common Requirements

summary.text: A metadata assertion's label shall end in .metadata or .metadata.ingredient, preceded by c2pa or an entity-specific namespace (for example com.litware.metadata). Each shall hold a single JSON content box with a JSON-LD serialization that includes @context, and the recommended approach is to build an XMP Data Model representation and serialize it to JSON-LD.

sections.extract: A metadata assertion shall have either a label which ends in the string .metadata or .metadata.ingredient and is preceded by either the standard c2pa identifier or any other provided that it conforms to the same syntax as entity-specific namespaces. For example, a com.litware.metadata assertion would be valid. NOTE: The .metadata.ingredient form supports related assertions to ingredients. Each metadata assertion

sections.title: 16.6.8.3. The c2pa.metadata assertion

summary.text: The block defines the c2pa.metadata assertion for a subset of common metadata schemas and requires claim generators to include only the fields enumerated in Appendix C, while custom-labelled metadata assertions may hold any values. JSON-LD examples show the assertion for an image (Exif, TIFF, IPTC and Photoshop fields including GPS data) and for a PDF.

sections.extract: This specification defines one metadata assertion, whose label is c2pa.metadata, which is used to represent a subset of common metadata schemas that may be used in any C2PA Manifest. Claim generators shall include in this assertion only the specific metadata fields enumerated in Appendix C, Implementation Details for c2pa.metadata. NOTE: Custom labelled metadata assertions can contain any values from any schemas.

sections.title: 16.6.8.4. Redaction of c2pa.metadata

summary.text: Although redaction removes only whole assertions, an update manifest allows partial redaction of c2pa.metadata by removing the original and adding a reduced version, which is then attributed to the update manifest's signer, for example keeping camera information while dropping location data.

sections.extract: Although the redaction process works in such a way that only an entire assertion could be redacted (see Section 8.8, “Redaction of Assertions”), the use of an update manifest enables partial redaction by removing the original and then placing the new, reduced, versions in the update manifest. This new assertion would be presented in a user experience in association with the signer of the update manifest and not with

sections.title: 16.7. Trust & Validation Adjuncts

summary.text: Introduction to Section 16.7, saying these assertions carry information used in manifest validation, such as certificate status, trusted time-stamps and session keys.

sections.extract: These assertions carry information used when validating a manifest, such as certificate status, trusted time-stamps, and session keys.

sections.title: 16.7.1. Certificate Status

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.7.1, Certificate Status; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.7.1.1. Description

summary.text: The certificate status assertion supplies trusted certificate revocation status after the fact for manifests created offline, where OCSP information could not be obtained at signing time.

sections.extract: In some provenance workflows, a standard or update manifest is created offline, where it is not possible to obtain the revocation information (via OCSP) at the time of signing. Without that information available during the validation process, a validator may need to go online to determine the revocation status of the certificate. This assertion is used to provide the trusted certificate status for such C2PA

sections.title: 16.7.1.2. Schema and Example

summary.text: The CDDL defines the certificate status map as a single ocspVals array of one or more byte strings, with a CBOR example.

sections.extract: The schema for this type is defined by the cert-status-map rule in the following CDDL Definition (see Section G.6.1, “Certificate Status” for the complete normative schema): certificate-status-map = { "ocspVals": [1* bstr] } An example in CBOR Diagnostic Format (.cbordiag) is shown below: { "ocspVals" : [ h'...', h'...' ] }

sections.title: 16.7.1.3. Requirements

summary.text: A certificate status assertion shall be labelled c2pa.certificate-status, appear at most once per manifest, and contain at least one ocspVals entry, storing the captured OCSP response in the same binary format used in the ocspVals array of the rVals header.

sections.extract: A certificate status assertion shall have a label of c2pa.certificate-status, and a C2PA Manifest shall contain at most one certificate status assertion. The certificate status assertion consists of a CBOR map (defined as a certificate-status-map) and shall contain at least one entry in the ocspVals array. As described in Section 13.5.2, “Certificate Revocation”, the claim generator queries the OCSP service

sections.title: 16.7.2. Time Stamps

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.7.2, Time Stamps; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.7.2.1. Description

summary.text: The time stamp assertion lets a trusted RFC 3161 time stamp be added later to a manifest created offline, before its signing certificate expires, giving proof of existence for the manifest and, for the active manifest, its asset.

sections.extract: In some provenance workflows, a standard or update manifest is created offline, where it is not possible to obtain a trusted time stamp (as per RFC 3161) from a TSA at the time of signing. However, in such cases those signing certificates will expire after a certain period of time, thus leading to an invalid C2PA Manifest. To prevent that expiration, a trusted time stamp can be added at a later point in time

sections.title: 16.7.2.2. Schema and Example

summary.text: The CDDL defines time-stamp-map as a map from C2PA manifest URNs to time stamp byte strings, with a CBOR example.

sections.extract: The schema for this type is defined by the time-stamp-map rule in the following CDDL Definition (see Section G.6.3, “Time Stamp” for the complete normative schema): ; The data structures used to store an array of ; manifest URNs to time stamp "blobs" $time-stamp-map /= { $time-stamp-entry => bstr } $time-stamp-entry /= tstr .regexp "^urn:c2pa:[\da-zA-Z_-]+$" An example in CBOR diagnostic notation (RFC 8949, clause

sections.title: 16.7.2.3. Requirements

summary.text: A time stamp assertion shall be labelled c2pa.time-stamp, appear at most once per manifest, and contain at least one entry keyed by the label of the manifest being time-stamped. Each value shall be the timeStampToken from an RFC 3161 TSA response obtained in detached mode by the usual process, except that the payload is the signature field of the target manifest's COSE_Sign1_Tagged claim signature.

sections.extract: A time stamp assertion shall have a label of c2pa.time-stamp, and there shall be at most one time stamp assertion per C2PA Manifest. The time stamp assertion consists of a CBOR map (defined as a time-stamp-map) which shall contain at least one key-value pair (defined as a time-stamp-entry). The key shall be the label of the C2PA Manifest receiving the time stamp, and the value shall be a CBOR byte string whose

sections.title: 16.7.3. Session Keys

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.7.3, Session Keys; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.7.3.1. Description

summary.text: The session keys assertion provides the keys used to sign the verifiable-segment-info-map in live media workflows based on the Verifiable Segment Info method, and is not required for workflows that rely only on the per-segment C2PA Manifest Box method.

sections.extract: This assertion provides the session keys that are used, as part of a live media workflow based on the "Section 15.5, “Verifiable Segment Info method”", to sign the verifiable-segment-info-map. Live media workflows that rely solely on the "Section 15.4, “Per-segment C2PA Manifest Box method”" are not required to use this assertion.

sections.title: 16.7.3.2. Requirements

summary.text: A session keys assertion shall be labelled c2pa.session-keys, at most one per manifest, and holds a keys array whose entries contain a COSE key with a kid, minSequenceNumber, createdAt, validityPeriod and a signerBinding signature over the signer's end-entity certificate. Keys shall be used only within their validity period, and new keys supplied in a later manifest may overlap earlier ones but their minSequenceNumber shall be at least the current sequence number, supporting key rotation and preventing replay.

sections.extract: A session keys assertion shall have a label of c2pa.session-keys, and a C2PA Manifest may contain at most one session keys assertion. The session keys assertion consists of a CBOR map (defined as a session-keys-data) and shall contain the following fields: keys An array of one or more session key objects. Each session key in the keys array is represented as an object containing the following fields: key A COSE key

sections.title: 16.7.3.3. Schema and Example

summary.text: The CDDL defines session-keys-data as an array of one or more session-key maps, each with a COSE key, minSequenceNumber, createdAt timestamp, validityPeriod in seconds and a COSE_Sign1_Tagged signerBinding. A CBOR example shows a c2pa.session-keys assertion with two P-256 keys.

sections.title: 16.8. Policy & Disclosure

summary.text: Introduction to Section 16.8, saying these assertions disclose policy-relevant characteristics of an asset, such as environmental impact and the role of generative AI or human oversight in its creation.

sections.extract: These assertions disclose policy-relevant characteristics of an asset, such as its environmental impact and the role of generative AI or human oversight in its creation.

sections.title: 16.8.1. Environmental Sustainability

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.8.1, Environmental Sustainability; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.8.1.1. Description

summary.text: The c2pa.environmental-sustainability assertion conveys machine-generated data on the environmental costs of creating or modifying an asset, a manifest may hold several, and their data may be aggregated, including recursively across ingredients. An action may reference one through relatedAssertions, and any such reference shall be a hashed JUMBF URI to an assertion in the same manifest. The optional energy_kwh, carbon_kgco2e (gross emissions, excluding offsets) and water_litres fields shall each hold a non-negative value in their named unit, and any measurementMethod shall be a reverse-DNS namespaced custom value.

sections.extract: The environmental sustainability assertion is used to convey machine-generated sustainability data associated with the creation or modification of an asset. The information carried by this assertion is intended to support transparency and auditing of environmental costs (for example, energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and water use) across a content supply chain, including workflows that use Generative

sections.title: 16.8.1.2. Schema and Example

summary.text: The CDDL defines environmental-sustainability-map with optional energy_kwh, carbon_kgco2e and water_litres measurement maps (a non-negative value and optional namespaced measurementMethod), metadata and custom fields. A CBOR example gives values for all three measures, though its caption describes a TensorFlow model, which does not match the example shown.

sections.extract: The schema for this type is defined by the environmental-sustainability-map rule in the following CDDL Definition (see Section G.5.13, “Environmental Sustainability” for the complete normative schema): ; The environmental sustainability assertion describes sustainability ; measurements associated with the creation or modification of an asset. environmental-sustainability-map = { ? "energy_kwh":

sections.title: 16.8.2. AI Disclosure

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.8.2, AI Disclosure; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.8.2.1. Summary

summary.text: The AI Disclosure assertion is introduced so claim generators can provide machine-readable, verifiable AI transparency information supporting automated compliance checks.

sections.extract: As part of an ongoing effort to enhance AI transparency and accountability, a new AI Disclosure assertion is introduced to provide a means for a Claim Generator to provide machine-readable AI transparency information. This assertion enables verifiable AI transparency, automated compliance verification, and trustworthy AI content at scale.

sections.title: 16.8.2.2. Details

summary.text: The AI Disclosure assertion shall be labelled c2pa.ai-disclosure and shall include modelType from the model type table, any scientificDomain shall follow the arXiv taxonomy, and other optional fields shall conform to the CDDL types.

sections.extract: The AI Disclosure assertion shall have a label of c2pa.ai-disclosure. The value of the modelType field is an enumeration of AI model types defined in Table 8, “Model type values” and it shall be present in the ai-model-disclosure-map object. If present, the value of the scientificDomain field shall conform to the arXiv taxonomy, e.g., "cs.AI", "physics.optics". All other fields are optional, but if present, they

sections.title: 16.8.2.3. Relationship Between digitalSourceType and humanOversightLevel

summary.text: The c2pa.ai-disclosure assertion complements c2pa.actions and digitalSourceType by adding model provenance, scientific domain metadata and a human oversight level. A table shows how digitalSourceType and humanOversightLevel combine, from fully autonomous AI generation to human-validated composites, and notes the assertion is not attached for digitalCreation with no trained model.

sections.extract: The c2pa.ai-disclosure assertion is designed to complement existing C2PA signals rather than replace them. In particular, c2pa.actions and digitalSourceType already provide a strong foundation for recording how an asset was created or modified. What this assertion introduces are three critical provenance primitives not previously captured in the ecosystem: model provenance — full disclosure of the AI models used for

sections.title: 16.8.2.4. Schema and Example

summary.text: The CDDL defines ai-model-disclosure-map with a required modelType, optional modelName, modelIdentifier, scientificDomain list and metadata, and a contentProfile holding humanOversightLevel with the values fully_autonomous, prompt_guided or human_validated; further fields are listed as pending. A CBOR example discloses a Hugging Face Transformers model, though its caption describes a TensorFlow model, which does not match the example shown.

sections.extract: The schema for this type is defined by the ai-model-disclosure-map rule in the following CDDL Definition (see Section G.5.14, “AI Disclosure” for the complete normative schema): ; CDDL Schema for AI Model Disclosure Metadata ai-model-disclosure-map = { "modelType": $model-type-choice, ; this is an enumeration of AI model types ? "modelName": tstr, ; human-readable name of the AI model used ; unique identifier of the

sections.title: 16.9. Assertion-Supporting Structures

summary.text: Introduction to Section 16.9, saying the structures that follow are used by the assertions above rather than being assertions themselves.

sections.extract: The following structures are used by the assertions defined above rather than being assertions in their own right.

sections.title: 16.9.1. Metadata About Assertions

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.9.1, Metadata About Assertions; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.9.1.1. Description

summary.text: Assertion metadata provides additional information about an assertion, such as when it was generated, to help Manifest Consumers judge its provenance, and consumers are not required to read any of it.

sections.extract: In many cases, it is useful or even necessary to provide additional information about an assertion, such as the date and time when it was generated or other data that may help Manifest Consumers to make informed decisions about the provenance or veracity of the assertion data. NOTE: A Manifest Consumer is not required to read any portion of assertion metadata. It can choose which, if any, fields it wishes to

sections.title: 16.9.1.2. Custom Values

summary.text: The assertion metadata structure may include custom key/value pairs, whose keys shall use entity-specific namespaces to avoid collisions.

sections.extract: The assertion metadata structure may include custom key/value pairs, in addition to the standard fields defined below. Such custom map keys shall be namespaced using the same entity-specific namespaces approach as described in Section 8.2.1, “Namespacing”. This ensures that there are no collisions between different organizations adding their own custom data.

sections.title: 16.9.1.3. Schema and Example

summary.text: The CDDL defines the assertion-metadata-map with optional dateTime, reviewRatings, reference, the deprecated dataSource (which claim generators shall not include), localizations, regionOfInterest, processStart, processEnd and custom fields. Supporting rules define bounded time maps with absolute, lowerBound or upperBound types, a source-map with a type and details, a rating-map with a value from 1 to 5, a code and explanation, and localization entries, followed by a CBOR example. Assertion metadata usually sits in another assertion's metadata field but can be stored separately in an assertion labelled c2pa.assertion.metadata, for example for non-JSON or non-CBOR assertions such as thumbnails.

sections.extract: Below shows the core schemas used inside other assertions. The CDDL Definition for the assertion-metadata-map rule is in the following listing (see Section G.7.1, “Assertion Metadata Common Types” for the complete normative schema): CDDL for Assertion Metadata ; Describes additional information about an assertion, including a hashed-uri ; reference to it. We use a socket/plug here to allow hashed-uri-map to be used

sections.title: 16.9.1.4. DateTime

summary.text: If present, dateTime shall be a CBOR-compliant date time string indicating when the assertion was generated.

sections.extract: If a dateTime field is present, its value shall be a date time string that complies with CBOR date/times (RFC 8949, 3.4.1). This field is used to indicate the date and time when the assertion was generated.

sections.title: 16.9.1.5. Region of Interest

summary.text: An assertion that applies to only part of an asset, such as a range of video frames or an image area, may identify that part with a regionOfInterest field holding a region-map object.

sections.extract: The assertion may be specific to only a portion of an asset - such as a range of frames in a video or a specific area on an image. Such a portion may be identified using a regionOfInterest field, whose value is a region-map object (as defined in Section 16.9.2, “Regions of Interest”).

sections.title: 16.9.1.6. Data Source

summary.text: Note stating that the dataSource field is deprecated, with a pointer to Section H.1.

sections.extract: NOTE: The dataSource field is deprecated. See Section H.1, “dataSource Field in Assertion Metadata”.

sections.title: 16.9.1.7. Review Ratings

summary.text: The optional reviewRatings array lets a claim generator attach one or more rating objects judging the quality of an assertion, and it shall not be present when a dataSource of type humanEntry.anonymous or humanEntry.credentialed is present. Each rating shall carry an integer value from 1 (worst) to 5 (best), with an optional human-readable explanation and an optional machine-readable code, drawn either from Table 11 (such as actions.unknownActionsPerformed, ingredient.notVisible or thumbnail.primaryMismatch) or from entity-specific namespaces.

sections.extract: When present, the reviewRatings array provides a place for the claim generator to provide one or more rating objects on the quality (or lack thereof) of an assertion. A reviewRatings shall not be present if a dataSource object is present with a type field whose value is either humanEntry.anonymous or humanEntry.credentialed. The value field of the rating object shall be present with any integer value from 1 (worst)

sections.title: 16.9.1.8. References

summary.text: Because the reference field of an assertion metadata assertion is a standard hashed_uri, it can point to assertions, and likewise claims, in manifests other than the active one, such as a c2pa.metadata assertion in an ingredient's manifest.

sections.extract: Because the reference field of the assertion metadata assertion is a standard hashed_uri, it is also possible to have an assertion metadata assertion refer to assertions in other manifests than the active one. For example, the active manifest may include an assertion metadata assertion that validates the c2pa.metadata assertion present in an ingredient’s manifest. NOTE: Since the claim is a special type of

sections.title: 16.9.1.9. Process time

summary.text: The optional processStart and processEnd fields describe the time span of the overall process behind the enclosing assertion, using generator lower-bound and upper-bound time types respectively, with processStart required to be no later than processEnd; a note says these are claim-generator timestamps, not trusted ones.

sections.extract: The optional processStart and processEnd fields describe the overall process represented by the enclosing assertion. As defined in Section 8.9, “Specifications of time in assertions”, processStart shall use generator-lower-bound-time-type, and processEnd shall use generator-upper-bound-time-type. When both fields are present, the time value represented by processStart shall be less than or equal to the time value

sections.title: 16.9.1.10. Localization

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.9.1.10, Localization; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.9.1.10.1. General

summary.text: The general localization text explains that, so consumers can read manifest information in their own language, localization information for an assertion can be added as a dictionary in the assertion's metadata.

sections.extract: It is important that consumers of C2PA manifests be able to understand the information in their native language, when possible. To this end, it is possible to add localization information for an assertion with a dictionary that is included in the assertion’s metadata.

sections.title: 16.9.1.10.2. Localization Dictionary

summary.text: A localization dictionary shall be a single object whose keys map to translations indexed by language in the JSON-LD style, with dot notation used for nested keys and [n] array indexing for array elements, as shown in examples translating dc:title and actions[0].softwareAgent. Third-party keys and values must be namespaced (for example com.litware), and claim generators should supply their human-readable strings this way, as in an example localizing custom actions in a c2pa.actions assertion's metadata.

sections.extract: A localization dictionary shall consist of a single object, where each of its keys represents the translations using the language indexing technique from JSON-LD. If the value that requires translation is not associated with a top-level key, then "dot notation" (.) shall be used to reference keys nested in objects. Array indexing notation ([n], n>=0) shall be used where a specific element in an array needs to be

sections.title: 16.9.2. Regions of Interest

summary.text: Heading that opens Section 16.9.2, Regions of Interest; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: 16.9.2.1. Description

summary.text: The description explains that some assertions, such as an actions assertion, apply only to part of an asset, and that a region definition is used to describe that temporal, spatial, textual or combined portion.

sections.extract: In some use cases, a given assertion, such as an actions assertion, may only be relevant to a specific portion of an asset as opposed to the entire asset. In those cases, it is necessary to have a way to describe that region - whether it be temporal, spatial, textual or a combination of them. A region definition serves that purpose.

sections.title: 16.9.2.2. Common

summary.text: The central part of a region is its range field, which may describe temporal, spatial, frame or textual ranges or a combination, though a note says how consumers use combinations is not yet defined. A region may also carry the common fields name, identifier, type (from a controlled vocabulary such as IPTC's or an entity-specific value) and description, while the older role field is deprecated and shall no longer be generated.

sections.extract: The most important part of the region definition is the range field which is used to describe a temporal range, a spatial range, a frame range, a textual range or a combination of them, for the region. NOTE: While the specification allows for specifying a combination of ranges, it is not defined how a Manifest Consumer will use them. It is expected that the C2PA’s User Experience Task Force will take this up in the

sections.title: 16.9.2.2.1. Ranges

summary.text: Every range has a type of spatial, temporal, frame, textual or identified, and shall contain the matching data object: shape, time, frame, text or item.

sections.extract: All ranges consist of a type field whose value is either "spatial", "temporal", "frame", "textual" or "identified". In addition, it shall contain one of the following fields whose data is an object consisting of the specific data for that range: shape (for spatial); time (for temporal); frame (for temporal or textual); text (for textual); item (for specifically identified items).

sections.title: 16.9.2.2.2. Spatial

summary.text: Spatial ranges use a shape object that can represent a rectangle, circle or polygon, modelled on the IPTC Region Boundary Structure.

sections.extract: Spatial ranges are described using a shape object. A shape can be used to represent a rectangle, a circle or a polygon. It is modelled on the Region Boundary Structure from the IPTC.

sections.title: 16.9.2.2.3. Temporal

summary.text: Temporal ranges use a time object running from a start to an end, expressed either as Normal Play Time (npt) relative to the start of the media or as absolute wall-clock time in RFC 3339 format, with npt the default and missing start or end values meaning the beginning or end of the asset; starts are inclusive and ends exclusive unless endInclusivity is set to inclusive. For wallClock ranges the end shall not precede the start and at least one shall be given, with the missing bound derived from the asset duration or, if unknown as in live streams, left open, and implementations should use minimal decimal precision and snap to the nearest earlier sample or frame where alignment matters.

sections.extract: Temporal ranges are described using a time object, which represents a range from a starting time to an ending time. Times are normally described using a value that is relative to the start of the media. This is commonly referred to as "Normal Play Time" (npt) as described in Section 4.4.2 of RFC 7826 (as recommended in W3C Media Fragments specification). Alternatively, it is possible to refer to an absolute time

sections.title: 16.9.2.2.4. Frames

summary.text: A frame object defines an inclusive range of zero-based frames or pages, defaulting to the whole asset when start or end are absent, and while often used for document pages it may serve other media, though temporal ranges are recommended for time-based media where possible.

sections.extract: A frame object defines a range using the starting and ending frames or pages (inclusive). If no start is provided, the range shall start at the beginning of the asset. If no end is provided, the range shall end at the end of the asset. If neither is provided, the range shall represent the entire asset. Frames are represented as a single ordinal numbers, where 0 is the first frame. While frames are typically used to

sections.title: 16.9.2.2.5. Textual

summary.text: A text object defines a range using one or more W3C Web Annotation fragment identifiers, optionally refined by inclusive start and end character offsets that default to the whole fragment. A text-selector-range-map pairs a selector with an optional end selector to form a contiguous range, and multiple pairs can describe a non-contiguous range.

sections.extract: A text object defines a range using a one or more URL fragment identifiers, as defined by the W3C Web Annotation fragment selector. It may also refine the range using offsets to the starting and ending characters (inclusive). If no start is provided, the range shall start at the beginning of the fragment. If no end is provided, the range shall end at the end of the fragment. If neither is provided, the range shall

sections.title: 16.9.2.2.6. Identified

summary.text: An item object identifies a track, media item or other discrete content item in the asset's container, using an identifier that should follow the container's naming scheme (track_id for MP4, item_ID for HEIF) and a value, so that for example track 2 of an MP4 could be singled out. Identified ranges can also name a region by a semantic value from an ontology such as the Foundational Model of Anatomy, in which case the identifier shall be the URL or URI of that schema.

sections.extract: An item object defines a media track, media item, or other discrete content item in the asset, allowing the claim generator to indicate assertions that apply to only a subset of the content carried in the asset’s file container. For example, it could be used to indicate that only the audio track of a video file is relevant. The media or content item is identified by an identifier string whose value should match the

sections.title: 16.9.2.3. Schema

summary.text: The block gives the CDDL schema for the region-map rule, pointing to Section G.5.10 for the complete normative version. It defines region-map with a required array of range-map entries plus optional name, identifier, type, deprecated role, description and metadata, and range-map with a type choice of spatial, temporal, frame, textual or identified and the corresponding shape, time, frame, text or item objects. Supporting rules define shape-map (rectangle, circle or polygon in pixel or percent units with origin, size, inside and vertices), npt and wallClock time maps with regex-constrained start and end and endInclusivity, frame-map, the text selector maps, and item-map with identifier and value.

sections.extract: The schema for this type is defined by the region-map rule in the following CDDL Definition (see Section G.5.10, “Regions of Interest” for the complete normative schema): region-map = { ; definition of the range, one or more ranges "region": [1* range-map], ; a free-text string representing a human-readable name for the region which ; could be used in a user interface. ? "name": tstr .size (1..max-tstr-length), ; a

sections.title: 16.9.2.4. Examples

summary.text: The block gives a series of region examples in CBOR diagnostic notation. They cover a combined temporal and spatial range in a video, textual ranges in DOCX, tagged and untagged PDF, Excel cells and table cells, a frame range for deleted PDF pages, a specific video track via an identified range, and an anatomy-based identified range spanning the whole asset.

sections.extract: A series of examples in CBOR diagnostic notation (RFC 8949, clause 8) are shown below: // example of a combined temporal and spatial range in a video // { "region": [ { "type": "temporal", "time": { "type": "npt", "start": "0", "end": "5.2" } }, { "type": "spatial", "shape": { "type": "rectangle", "unit": "pixel", "origin": { "x": 10.0, "y": 10.0 }, "width": 200.0, "height": 112.0 } } ], "name": "Animated Logo",

sections.title: 17. Patent Policy

summary.text: The patent policy states that the C2PA follows the W3C Patent Policy (2004), with each Working Group Participant committing to license its Essential Claims in Approved Deliverables on W3C royalty-free terms, while source code is covered by the Working Group charter licence. Before a draft is approved a participant may exclude Essential Claims by written Exclusion Notice to the chair, identifying the patents or applications concerned, with any claims not listed remaining under the commitment and the chair publishing the notices.

sections.extract: The C2PA has adopted an open standard patent policy via W3C’s Patent Mode (2004): Licensing Commitment. For materials other than source code or datasets developed by the Working Group, each Working Group Participant agrees to make available any of its Essential Claims, as defined in the W3C Patent Policy (available at http://www.w3.org/Consortium/Patent-Policy-20040205), under the W3C RF licensing requirements

sections.title: Appendix A: Embedding manifests

summary.text: Heading that opens Appendix A, Embedding manifests; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: A.1. Supported Formats

summary.text: The supported formats section says a C2PA Manifest is embedded as part of the asset's C2PA Manifest Store, whose location depends on the asset's format. It provides an alphabetical table mapping each well-known format, from append-only text files, AVI and DNG through JPEG, MP4, PDF, PNG, SVG, TTML, WARC, WebP and WebVTT, to its IANA media type, normative reference and the specification section that defines its embedding. Notes say native FLAC is under consideration and explain that a dash means no registered IANA media type or no cited normative reference.

sections.extract: A C2PA Manifest is embedded into an asset as part of the C2PA Manifest Store for that asset. When embedding the C2PA Manifest Store into an asset, the location will vary based on the type or format of the asset. The table below indexes well-known file formats, sorted alphabetically, by their IANA Media Type (where one is officially registered), their normative reference (where this specification cites one), and the

sections.title: A.2. Embedding manifests in multi-part assets

summary.text: For a multi-part asset, a C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded in the primary part, containing the active manifest, whose multi-asset hash assertion shall give the location and hash of each part and should describe the provenance of the whole, while other parts may carry their own stores.

sections.extract: When embedding a C2PA Manifest into a multi-part asset ("multi-asset"), there shall be a C2PA Manifest Store embedded into the primary part of the asset (which contains the active manifest), though additional parts may also contain their own C2PA Manifest Stores. The active manifest of the primary part shall contain a multi-asset hash assertion that describes the location and hash of each part within the asset and

sections.title: A.3. Embedding manifests into non-BMFF-based assets

summary.text: Heading that opens Section A.3, Embedding manifests into non-BMFF-based assets; the block holds no text beyond the heading.

sections.title: A.3.1. Embedding manifests into JPEG 1

summary.text: In JPEG 1 the C2PA Manifest Store shall be carried in APP11 marker segments, written as multiple sequential, contiguous segments when it exceeds the 64K segment limit, with the same method applied to Exif compressed files and, for CIPA Multi-Picture Format assets, to the APP11 segment of the first image.

sections.extract: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded as the data contained in an APP11 marker segment as defined in ISO/IEC 18477-3. Since a single marker segment in JPEG 1 cannot be larger than 64K bytes, it is likely that multiple APP11 segments will be required, and they shall be constructed as per the JPEG 1 standard and ISO 19566-5:2023, D.2. When writing multiple segments, they shall be written in sequential order, and

sections.title: A.3.2. Embedding manifests into PNG

summary.text: In PNG the C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded in an ancillary, private, not-safe-to-copy chunk of type caBX that precedes the IDAT chunks.

sections.extract: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded using an ancillary, private, not safe to copy, chunk type of 'caBX' (as per PNG, clause 5.4). The 'caBX' chunk shall precede the 'IDAT' chunks.

sections.title: A.3.3. Embedding manifests into SVG

summary.text: For SVG, the binary C2PA Manifest Store must be Base64-encoded, though an external manifest is preferred. When embedded it shall be the value of a c2pa:manifest element inside the SVG metadata element, and an xmlns:c2pa namespace declaration should be added to the svg element, as an example shows.

sections.extract: SVG is an XML-based format that can exist either stand-alone or embedded into other text-based formats such as HTML. As such, it is necessary to Base64 encode the binary C2PA Manifest Store to perform the embedding. While this section describes how to do that, the use of an external manifest is preferred. The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded as the Base64-encoded value of a c2pa:manifest element in the metadata

sections.title: A.3.4. Embedding manifests into TTML

summary.text: For standalone TTML files (application/ttml+xml) the C2PA Manifest Store shall be Base64-encoded in a c2pa:manifest element at /tt:tt/tt:head/tt:metadata/c2pa:manifest with the c2pa namespace declared on the root element, whereas TTML carried inside a BMFF container uses the BMFF embedding instead, and an external manifest is preferred where toolchains drop foreign-namespace elements. Implementations shall not treat this element as a conformance error even in constrained profiles such as IMSC or EBU-TT-D, and the claim generator shall include a c2pa.hash.data assertion whose single exclusion range covers the c2pa:manifest element from opening to closing tag.

sections.extract: TTML2 (Timed Text Markup Language) is an XML-based format for timed text (subtitles and captions) defined by the W3C. This section applies only to standalone TTML files with the media type application/ttml+xml. When TTML is carried as a timed-text track inside a BMFF-based container (e.g., MP4 or IMF), the C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded in the outer BMFF container as described in Section A.5, “Embedding

sections.title: A.3.5. Embedding manifests into ID3

summary.text: In ID3v2-compatible audio files such as MP3 or FLAC, the C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded as the encapsulated data of a General Encapsulated Object (GEOB) whose MIME type field is set to the JUMBF media type.

sections.extract: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded into a ID3v2-compatible, compressed audio file (e.g., MP3 or FLAC) file as the Encapsulated object data of a General Encapsulated Object (GEOB) as defined in ID3. The GEOB’s MIME type field shall be present and shall use the value for the media type for JUMBF as described in Section 11.8, “External Manifests”. <a

sections.title: A.3.6. Embedding manifests into Standard MIDI Files (MIDI 1.0)

summary.text: The section introduces embedding in Standard MIDI Files, describing their MThd header and MTrk track chunks and the Sequencer-Specific Meta Event (FF 7F) for application data, and notes that MIDI 2.0 Clip Files are not covered.

sections.extract: Standard MIDI Files (Standard MIDI Files 1.0) are composed of a header chunk (MThd) followed by one or more track chunks (MTrk). Each track chunk contains a sequence of MIDI events, including Meta Events (identified by the status byte 0xFF). The Sequencer-Specific Meta Event (FF 7F) is defined by Standard MIDI Files 1.0 for application-specific binary data, using a manufacturer identifier in its data field. NOTE:

sections.title: A.3.6.1. C2PA Manifest Store embedding

summary.text: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded as an FF 7F Sequencer-Specific Meta Event placed just before the End of Track event in a designated track (the sole track for Format 0, the last for Format 1, the first for Format 2), with its data starting with the extended manufacturer identifier 0x00 0x43 0x32 followed by the store bytes. Only one such event is allowed, with duplicates meaning no manifest is treated as located, and the inserted event shall have delta-time 0 while any non-zero delta-time from the original End of Track moves to the following FF 2F event so track duration is unchanged.

sections.extract: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded as a Sequencer-Specific Meta Event (FF 7F) placed immediately before the End of Track event (FF 2F) in the designated track chunk: For Format 0 files (single track): the sole MTrk chunk. For Format 1 files (multi-track): the last MTrk chunk. For Format 2 files (multiple independent patterns): the first MTrk chunk. The data field of the FF 7F event shall begin with the 3-byte

sections.title: A.3.6.2. Locating the Manifest Store

summary.text: A validator shall locate the manifest store by parsing MThd for the file format, picking the designated track, scanning it to End of Track for an FF 7F event starting with 0x00 0x43 0x32 whose remaining bytes are the store, and treating the asset as having no manifest if none is found.

sections.extract: A validator shall locate the C2PA Manifest Store in a Standard MIDI File as follows: 1. Parse the MThd chunk to determine the file format (0, 1, or 2) and the total number of track chunks. 2. Identify the designated track chunk: for Format 0, the sole track; for Format 1, the last track; for Format 2, the first track. 3. Scan the events of the designated track sequentially until the End of Track event (FF 2F) is

sections.title: A.3.6.3. Data hash binding

summary.text: A claim generator shall include a c2pa.hash.data assertion whose single exclusion range covers only the C2PA Manifest Store bytes following the manufacturer identifier, while the FF 7F status bytes, length field and identifier stay inside the hash and unchanged between passes.

sections.extract: A claim generator embedding a manifest in a Standard MIDI File shall include a c2pa.hash.data assertion with a single exclusion range: start: the byte offset within the file of the first byte of the C2PA Manifest Store (i.e., the byte immediately after the 0x00 0x43 0x32 extended manufacturer identifier within the FF 7F data field) length: the byte length of the C2PA Manifest Store The FF 7F status bytes, the

sections.title: A.3.6.4. Writing a Manifest Store

summary.text: Writing a manifest store into a MIDI file reserves a placeholder FF 7F event before End of Track, hashes the file excluding the placeholder, signs, and then replaces the placeholder with the signed store of identical length, keeping the event's length field and its encoding unchanged.

sections.extract: To embed a C2PA Manifest Store: 1. Reserve an FF 7F event in the designated track immediately before the FF 2F End of Track event, with a data field consisting of the 3-byte extended manufacturer identifier 0x00 0x43 0x32 followed by a placeholder C2PA Manifest Store of the required size. 2. Compute the data hash over the complete file with the placeholder manifest store bytes excluded. 3. Sign the manifest using

sections.title: A.3.6.5. Re-embedding a Manifest Store

summary.text: When re-embedding a manifest store of a different size, the existing FF 7F event cannot be patched in place, so the claim generator shall remove it, reserve a new one before End of Track, recompute the designated track chunk's 4-byte length, and repeat the two-pass hash, sign and replace flow. A note explains that because offsets are recomputed each pass, update manifests need not stay at a fixed file offset, unlike TIFF.

sections.extract: When a new C2PA Manifest Store of a different size is written into a file that already contains one, the existing FF 7F event cannot be patched in place — the designated track chunk’s 4-byte length field shall be updated to reflect the new byte layout. Because the designated track is identified structurally (the sole track for Format 0, the last track for Format 1, or the first track for Format 2) rather than by a

sections.title: A.3.7. Embedding manifests into OGG Vorbis

summary.text: In Ogg Vorbis the C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded in its own logical bitstream whose first packet begins with the 5-byte identifier \x00c2pa followed by the store data.

sections.extract: Ogg Vorbis (as described in RFC 3533) is an open-source, lossy audio compression format encapsulated within the Ogg multimedia container. The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded in its own dedicated logical bitstream within the container. The first packet of this stream starts with the 5-byte identifier \x00c2pa, and the C2PA Manifest Store data follows immediately after. <a

sections.title: A.3.8. Embedding manifests into TIFF-based assets

summary.text: For TIFF-based files, including Exif uncompressed, TIFF/EP, DNG and other TIFF-based RAW formats, the C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded as the data of tag 52545 (0xCD41) with tag type 7, and the TIFF ByteOrder does not govern its endianness. There shall be only one store per asset, placed in the last IFD of the main chain (in the single main IFD or a new IFD after it, otherwise as the only entry in its IFD), and it should sit at the end of the file to support update manifests without disturbing other offsets.

sections.extract: The DNG format provides camera manufacturers to provide their camera raw formats in a standardized manner. DNG is based on which is based on TIFF/EP (which is, itself, based on TIFF v6). An Exif uncompressed file (Exif, Section 3.2) is also based on TIFF. The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded into a TIFF-compatible file (i.e., Exif uncompressed file (Exif, Section 3.2), TIFF/EP, DNG or other TIFF-based RAW

sections.title: A.3.9. Embedding manifests into RIFF-based assets

summary.text: In RIFF-based files such as WAV, BWF, AVI and WebP, the C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded as the data of a chunk with identifier C2PA that is the last sub-chunk of the first RIFF header chunk.

sections.extract: The RIFF format provides a generic container format for storing data in tagged chunks. It is primarily used to store multimedia such as images, sound and video. It serves as the container format for WAV, BWF, Broadcast Wave, AVI and WebP. NOTE: RIFF is based on an older format called IFF. The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded into a RIFF-compatible file (i.e., WAV, AVI or WebP) as the data of a chunk with an

sections.title: A.3.10. Embedding manifests into GIFs

summary.text: In GIF the C2PA Manifest Store shall be split into data sub-blocks of at most 255 bytes inside a single Application Extension block with identifier C2PA_GIF, whose Application Authentication Code serves as a block version (initially 1.0). The block layout is given in full and the block shall be placed after the header and before the first image descriptor.

sections.extract: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be broken into chunks of a size no greater than 255 bytes and embedded into contiguous data sub-blocks (as per GIF, 15) within a C2PA-specialised Application Extension block (as per GIF, 26), specified below. NOTE: In this C2PA Application Extension Block, the Application Authentication Code is not used to authenticate the application producing the block. Instead, it is used as a block

sections.title: A.3.11. Embedding manifests into JPEG XL

summary.text: A JPEG XL file using the box structure shall contain at most one top-level JUMBF superbox holding the C2PA Manifest Store, not shared with other JUMBF boxes, while a bare JPEG XL codestream cannot carry an embedded manifest, as an accompanying figure illustrates.

sections.extract: As described in ISO/IEC 18181-2:2024, Clause 4, JPEG XL supports two different formats for the data. It may use a box structure that is compatible with JPEG 2000 and JPEG XS or it may be a direct JPEG XL codestream without the box structure. A JPEG XL file that uses the box structure shall contain at most one JUMBF (jumb) superbox (ISO/IEC 18181-2:2024, Clause 9.3) containing one C2PA Manifest JUMBF Box, which

sections.title: A.3.12. Embedding manifests into fonts

summary.text: Fonts conforming to Open Font Format or OpenType may include a C2PA table holding an embedded manifest, a remote manifest URI or both, and the block notes that the table's definition that follows is preliminary.

sections.extract: Fonts which conform to either Open Font Format or the OpenType specification may include a C2PA table. When present, this table may include an embedded manifest, a remote manifest URI, or both. The C2PA table format is not yet defined in the Open Font Format nor OpenType specification; the following definition is preliminary:

sections.title: A.3.12.1. Table Tag

summary.text: The C2PA font table is identified by the table tag C2PA.

sections.extract: The C2PA table record will be identified by the following table tag: C2PA.

sections.title: A.3.12.2. Table Record

summary.text: The C2PA font table record, given in Table 12, supports embedded, remote or both kinds of manifest store through the fields majorVersion, minorVersion, activeManifestUriOffset, activeManifestUriLength, reserved, manifestStoreOffset and manifestStoreLength, with a NULL offset recommended when a URI or store is absent. A non-embedded manifest may be remote or on the same storage system, and a JUMBF URI reference should be valid within the store.

sections.extract: The C2PA table provides full support for a Manifest Stores to be either embedded or remote or both. The table record is defined as follows: Table 12. C2PA table record Type; Name; Description uint16; majorVersion; Specifies the major version of the C2PA font table. uint16; minorVersion; Specifies the minor version of the C2PA font table. Offset32; activeManifestUriOffset; Offset from the beginning of the C2PA font

sections.title: A.3.13. Embedding manifests into .facti/.facta/.factv

summary.text: The section introduces the IANA-registered BlockFact container formats .facti, .facta and .factv, listing their media types and describing their layout of a fixed header, JSON metadata with format_version and media_length, a media payload and typed extension blocks.

sections.extract: The BlockFact family of formats (.facti, .facta, .factv) are IANA-registered binary container formats for provenance-verified media. The full format specification is available at blockfact.io/docs/facti-format-spec. image/vnd.blockfact.facti — https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/image/vnd.blockfact.facti audio/vnd.blockfact.facta — https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/audio/vnd.blockfact.facta

sections.title: A.3.13.1. C2PA Manifest Store embedding

summary.text: In these formats the C2PA Manifest Store shall be stored, without extra framing, as the data of an extension block of type C2PA.

sections.extract: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be embedded as the data of an extension block with the 4-byte ASCII type identifier C2PA (0x43 0x32 0x50 0x41). The block data is a complete C2PA Manifest Store with no additional framing or transformation.

sections.title: A.3.13.2. Locating the Manifest Store

summary.text: Extracting the manifest store involves reading the magic bytes and metadata length, parsing the JSON metadata for media_length, skipping the media payload, and iterating the extension blocks to find the one of type C2PA.

sections.extract: To extract the C2PA Manifest Store: 1. Read and verify the magic bytes (4 bytes). 2. Read the metadata length N (4 bytes, big-endian). 3. Parse the JSON metadata (N bytes) to obtain media_length (M). 4. Skip the media payload (M bytes). 5. Read the extension block count (2 bytes, big-endian). 6. Iterate extension blocks: for each, read type (4 bytes) + length L (4 bytes) + data (L bytes). 7. The block with type C2PA

sections.title: A.3.13.3. Data hash binding

summary.text: The c2pa.hash.data assertion shall cover the whole file with a single exclusion range spanning the C2PA block's data, beginning just after its type and length fields.

sections.extract: The c2pa.hash.data assertion shall reference the entire file with a single exclusion range covering the C2PA block data: start: byte offset of the C2PA block data (immediately after the block’s 4-byte type and 4-byte length fields) length: byte length of the C2PA block data

sections.title: A.3.13.4. Writing a Manifest Store

summary.text: Writing follows the usual placeholder, hash, sign and same-length replace flow, only one C2PA block is allowed per file (duplicates mean no manifest is treated as located), and consumers shall ignore unrecognised extension block types.

sections.extract: To embed a C2PA Manifest Store: 1. Construct the file with a placeholder C2PA extension block of the required reserved size. 2. Compute the data hash over the complete file with the placeholder region excluded. 3. Sign the manifest using the computed data hash. 4. sections.title: A.3.14. Embedding manifests into Parquet

summary.text: The section introduces Apache Parquet, describing its row groups and Thrift-encoded FileMetaData footer with optional key_value_metadata and trailing length and PAR1 magic number, and notes that manifests can only be embedded in non-encrypted Parquet files.

sections.extract: Apache Parquet File Format is a columnar storage format widely used for structured and semi-structured data, such as analytics and machine-learning datasets. A Parquet file consists of one or more row groups of column-chunk data followed by a footer containing a Thrift-encoded FileMetaData structure that describes the file’s schema, row groups, and an optional key_value_metadata list of arbitrary key/value pairs.

sections.title: A.3.14.1. C2PA Manifest Store embedding

summary.text: In Parquet the C2PA Manifest Store shall be Base64-encoded and stored as the value of a single key_value_metadata entry with key c2pa:manifest in the footer's FileMetaData, with more than one such entry meaning no manifest is treated as located.

sections.extract: The value of a KeyValue entry in key_value_metadata is a Thrift string (i.e., UTF-8 text). The C2PA Manifest Store shall therefore be Base64-encoded (per RFC 4648) and embedded as the value of a KeyValue entry in the key_value_metadata list of the footer’s FileMetaData, using a key of c2pa:manifest. Only one KeyValue entry with a key of c2pa:manifest shall be present per file. If more than one such entry is

sections.title: A.3.14.2. Data hash binding

summary.text: A claim generator shall include a c2pa.hash.data assertion whose single exclusion range covers only the Base64-encoded value bytes of the c2pa:manifest entry in the serialized footer.

sections.extract: A claim generator embedding a manifest in a Parquet file shall include a c2pa.hash.data assertion with a single exclusion range covering the Base64-encoded value bytes of the c2pa:manifest KeyValue entry within the serialized footer. NOTE: This means that the prefix is not part of the exclusion range.

sections.title: A.3.14.3. Writing a Manifest Store

summary.text: Writing a manifest into Parquet reserves a placeholder c2pa:manifest entry, hashes the file with the placeholder excluded, signs, and replaces the value with the same-length encoded manifest, so the footer length stays valid. Since Parquet libraries usually rewrite footers wholesale, claim generators should check that their writer preserves the entry's exact byte length and the order of key_value_metadata entries.

summary.text: The section introduces ONNX as a format for trained machine learning models, consisting of a Protocol Buffers-encoded ModelProto whose metadata_props field holds key/value pairs.

sections.extract: ONNX Intermediate Representation Specification, Version 10 is a widely used format for representing trained machine learning models. summary.text: In ONNX the C2PA Manifest Store shall be Base64-encoded and stored as the value of a single metadata_props entry with key c2pa:manifest, with more than one such entry meaning no manifest is treated as located.

sections.extract: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be Base64-encoded (per RFC 4648) and stored as the value of a StringStringEntryProto entry in the ModelProto.metadata_props list, using a key of c2pa:manifest. Only one entry with a key of c2pa:manifest shall be present per model file. If more than one such entry is encountered, the asset shall be treated as if no manifests were located.

sections.title: A.3.16. Embedding manifests into SafeTensors

summary.text: Introduces the SafeTensors format, describing its layout as an 8-byte little-endian header length, a UTF-8 JSON header with a __metadata__ object of string key/value pairs, and then raw tensor data.

sections.extract: SafeTensors Format Specification is a format for storing tensors safely (without arbitrary code execution) and efficiently. A SafeTensors file begins with an 8-byte little-endian unsigned integer specifying the length of a JSON header, followed by the UTF-8 JSON header itself, followed by the raw tensor data. The JSON header contains a metadata key whose value is an object of arbitrary string key/value pairs. <a

sections.title: A.3.16.1. C2PA Manifest Store embedding

summary.text: In SafeTensors, the Manifest Store shall be Base64-encoded and stored under a single c2pa:manifest key in the __metadata__ object, and if more than one such key is present the asset shall be treated as having no manifests.

sections.extract: The C2PA Manifest Store shall be Base64-encoded (per RFC 4648) and stored as the value of a c2pa:manifest key within the metadata object of the SafeTensors JSON header. Only one c2pa:manifest key shall be present in the metadata object. If more than one is encountered, the asset shall be treated as if no manifests were located.

sections.title: A.3.16.2. Data hash binding

summary.text: A claim generator embedding a manifest in a SafeTensors file shall include a c2pa.hash.data assertion with one exclusion range covering the Base64 value bytes of the c2pa:manifest entry.

sections.extract: A claim generator embedding a manifest in a SafeTensors file shall include a c2pa.hash.data assertion with a single exclusion range covering the Base64-encoded value bytes of the c2pa:manifest entry within the JSON header.

sections.title: A.3.16.3. Writing a Manifest Store

summary.text: For SafeTensors, a two-pass procedure shall be used: reserve a placeholder c2pa:manifest key in __metadata__, hash the whole file (length field, JSON header and tensor data) excluding the placeholder, sign, then substitute the signed manifest at the same encoded length. sections.title: A.3.17. Embedding manifests into append-only text files

summary.text: Introduces the method for append-only text files, in which provenance is attached through a rolling chain of signed checkpoints, each covering a bounded segment of new content and cryptographically linked to the previous one so a validator can verify the file's full history.

sections.extract: Plain-text files are commonly written in an append-only fashion: new lines are added at the end and existing content is never modified. This section defines how to associate C2PA provenance with such files using a rolling chain of signed checkpoints. Each checkpoint covers a bounded segment of new content and is cryptographically linked to the previous checkpoint, enabling a validator to verify the complete history

sections.title: A.3.17.1. Applicability

summary.text: The method applies only to files written by appending complete lines and never rewriting earlier bytes, namely plain-text logs (text/plain) and JSON Lines streams; CSV and TSV shall instead use an external manifest, and structured text such as source code, configuration, Markdown and YAML shall use the structured text embedding method. A file with checkpoints shall not also carry a structured text manifest block, and the two methods are told apart by the sentinel delimiters (BEGIN C2PA CHECKPOINT versus BEGIN C2PA MANIFEST).

sections.extract: This section applies to files that are written only by appending complete lines to the end of the file, and whose earlier bytes are never rewritten, specifically: Plain-text files with no structural record grammar, such as application logs and event logs (text/plain). sections.title: A.3.17.2. Sentinel line

summary.text: Each checkpoint shall be exactly one sentinel line appended right after its segment, delimited by -----BEGIN C2PA CHECKPOINT----- and -----END C2PA CHECKPOINT----- in plain text or written as a JSON object with a c2pa:checkpoint member in JSONL, and holding either an external URI to the Manifest Store or an inline data:application/c2pa;base64 URI, both of which validators shall accept. A file may hold many sentinel lines, and the one at the highest byte offset is the active checkpoint.

sections.extract: Each checkpoint shall be represented by exactly one sentinel line, appended immediately after the last line of the segment it covers, as a complete line terminated by the file’s line-ending convention. The sentinel line shall either reference the C2PA Manifest Store by an external URI or embed it inline as a data: URI (RFC 2397). summary.text: A checkpoint shall use a c2pa.hash.segment assertion as its hard binding, not c2pa.hash.data, and an example assertion with segmentStart, segmentEnd, sentinelLength and predecessorSentinel fields is given for a CRLF file.

sections.extract: A claim generator creating a checkpoint shall include a c2pa.hash.segment assertion, which is the hard binding for the segment that checkpoint covers. A checkpoint manifest shall not use a c2pa.hash.data assertion for this purpose. summary.text: Each checkpoint manifest shall reference the immediately preceding checkpoint manifest as a parentOf ingredient, except the first checkpoint, and chain verification rules are deferred to the segment hash validation section.

sections.extract: Each checkpoint manifest shall reference the immediately preceding checkpoint manifest as a parentOf ingredient. The first checkpoint in a file has no predecessor and shall not include a parentOf ingredient for this purpose. The rules for verifying a chain of checkpoints are defined in Section 14.12.6, “Validating a segment hash”.

It then builds the c2pa.hash.segment assertion from these values and signs and stores the Manifest Store at the chosen URI, so the sentinel append is the only file write, which suits WORM and append-only storage.

sections.title: A.3.17.5.2. Inline form

Omitting sentinelLength removes the circular dependency between the manifest and the sentinel's length, keeping the procedure compatible with WORM and append-only storage.

sections.title: A.4.2.1. Adding the Manifest to a PDF

summary.text: For a document-level manifest, the PDF catalog shall have an AF entry referencing only the embedded file specification holding the active manifest's store, also referenced from the EmbeddedFiles name tree or a FileAttachment annotation, with the annotation route required when a certifying signature exists so DocMDP restrictions are not broken. The manifest shall be attached as close as possible to the object that actually stores the described data, for example the Image XObject stream or font file stream.

summary.text: Merkle-purpose boxes carry CBOR-encoded hashes and tree proofs for Merkle-tree based validation.

sections.title: A.5.3.1. General

summary.text: Explains that large or fragmented BMFF assets use multiple hashes so parts can be validated without downloading every 'mdat', and that Merkle trees (one per 'mdat' in non-fragmented files, one per track in fragmented ones) keep the manifest small, with the manifest storing one tree row and an auxiliary box per subset giving its leaf position and the extra hashes needed. The choice of row trades manifest size against auxiliary box size and is left to the implementation, but the BMFF Hash portion of the manifest shall include the merkle field.

sections.extract: Some files have one or more very large 'mdat' boxes (e.g., large video or image files which may be downloaded and rendered progressively) or large numbers of independent 'mdat' boxes (e.g., fMP4 where each fragment can be downloaded independently). summary.text: For a non-fragmented asset, two or more merkle boxes shall follow the last 'mdat' when the manifest holds a non-leaf row, with leaf hashes computed over 'mdat' payload subsets sized by fixedBlockSize or variableBlockSizes. The boxes shall follow subset order, be grouped contiguously per tree, and carry location values counting up from 0.

They are not required to be included in the file if the manifest contains the leaf row of the merkle tree. If they exist, they shall follow the last 'mdat' box in the file. Concatenating split files does not yield a compliant file, so producing both forms shall treat the first as a parentOf ingredient with a c2pa.repackaged action.

summary.text: Because some IDs such as the 'tkhd' track_id are only locally unique, a unique ID defined at manifest creation is combined with the local ID to make a globally unique identifier. A note explains that fixed-size merkle boxes let a progressively downloading client compute the offset of the box it needs and fetch only that box.

This unique ID does not equal any value from the original asset; each value is instead defined when the manifest is created.
